    Electric motors are obviously immune to carburetor ice, or to water and
ice in the fuel tanks. Electric motors are easy to start: just feed them power.
The motors are safer than fuel-based engines, having no fuel for fires, no
carbon-monoxide emissions, and little potential for spraying fuel or hot oil
around. Sometimes, though, the batteries catch fire.
    Electric motors can be deliberately overpowered for a short time, gener­
ating as much as three times their normal power (25% boost is more typical).
   * The subsection title comes from the ancient and humorously derogatory designation applied to
aircr aft electrical/avionics engineers, namely "Sparkies."
740    A i rc raft Des i g n : A Conceptu a l A p p roach


         This can be used for takeoff or emergency power and allows a motor with
         lower rated power than an equivalent gasoline engine. Electric motors
         don't lose power with altitude (although fuel cells do). Electric aircraft als o
        have a fairly flat torque-vs-rpm curve which makes it easier to use them
         for flight control, compared to fuel-burning engines.
             Aircraft configuration flexibility is enhanced with the use of electric pro­
        pulsion. The motors are small and can be placed far away from the power
        supply. It has been proposed to use electrical generators and motors to remo­
        tely locate the fans of turbofan engines out to the wings or another location
        deemed beneficial. Some electric aircraft designs use multiple small motors
        on the wing and feed them varying amounts of power to attain yaw
        control. In fact, most quadcopters have no controls at all other than
        varying the power to their four motors.
             Electric motors themselves have always been lighter than internal
        combustion engines and are getting even better. Thanks to the increased
        interest and research in aircraft electric power plants, the weight per unit
       power of motor plus housing and inverter has been halved in the last decade.
             There can even be a weight savings for the propeller. For a piston engine,
       the propeller is used as a flywheel to help damp out the intermittent "bangs"
       of the cylinders. This might require additional mass in the propeller that is
       avoided with an electric motor. Also, if a propeller extension shaft is used
       with a piston engine, that shaft will be prone to torsional excitation and
       will have to be made stronger and heavier as a result. Not so with an electric
       motor. Furthermore, the electric motor is smaller and it might be possible to
       move the motor closer to the propeller, eliminating the need for a shaft in the
       first place. At the least, the smaller size of an electric motor should allow a
       more streamlined cowling.
            There are, of course, disadvantages or we would have been using them for
      years. While the motors are lighter, the total weight including the power
       supply is almost certainly heavier than an equivalent power, equivalent
       run-time internal combustion engine.
            It usually takes longer to "refuel" an electric airplane, that is, recharge the
      batteries. Progress is being made both in recharge time and in alternative
      concepts such as fuel cells that don't involve recharging, but it is still a lot
      quicker to refill gas tanks.
            Electric propulsion systems currently cost more, especially if an exotic
      power supply is used. The counter argument is that the "fuel" cost per
      flight hour is much cheaper than gasoline so in effect, you are "purchasing"
      your fuel in advance.
            The electric motors often need reduction drives due to their high rpm,
      which adds to the weight, cost, and complexity. Geared reduction drives
      can make quite a bit of noise.
            A subtle disadvantage is that, unlike fuel-based powerplants, there is no
      range benefit from the burn off of "fuel" during the mission. At the end of
      cruise, the gas-powered aircraft is lighter and therefore has less drag. It is
                                                 C H A PT E R 20   Electri c Ai rcraft   74 1


th is effect that is integrated in the Breguet range equation, but it does not
ap ply to electric propulsion. Instead, drag stays the same and the range is
fo und simply as speed times the power supply's calculated duration. For a
lo ng-range aircraft this may be equivalent to a 10-20% reduction in range.
     For battery power systems there are additional problems. There are temp­
erature effects on the batteries, with loss of power if too hot or too cold.
Attempting to use the power at too high of a rate causes resistance losses,
which reduces the total energy available. There is some risk of explosion
and fire for certain battery types. Imagine all of the energy stored in a big
battery being released all at once! And as every child with a flashlight has
learned, batteries tend to lose power as they reach the end of their
charge-just when we may need maximum power for a landing go-around.
     Batteries don't last forever. They are limited both in calendar age and in
total number of charge-discharge cycles. Complete battery replacement
might be required every 5-8 years, or sooner if the plane is flown a lot.
Most of us have experienced a perfectly good cellphone or laptop computer
needing a battery replacement, and finding that the replacement cost is so
high that a new unit is purchased instead.
     Hopefully this won't apply to electric airplanes. Toyota claims that not a
single Prius automobile has required battery replacement due to failure to
hold a charge. Toyota gets maximum life by ensuring that the batteries are
never fully charged, nor fully discharged. This is probably not an option
for airplanes, where weight is so important that we cannot afford to oversize
the battery pack as required by this strategy.
     Electric motors also put out a lot of stray electromagnetic energy which
can cause problems with other electronic components. This author witnessed
the tragic demise of a 32-foot-span unmanned research airplane constructed
as a senior design project. [2] This crashed because the electric motor
interfered with the radio �ignals, including the signal to turn off the motor!
     Electric power might not even be as "green" as imagined, when all things
are considered. Any electrical power source other than solar cells will need to
be charged or replenished. This means that there will be a ground facility
somewhere creating that energy, probably from burning hydrocarbon coal,
oil, or natural gas. This off-vehicle pollution must be included in an honest
system-level study of just how green an electric-powered airplane might
be. Some skeptics prefer to call them "remote emission" rather than "zero
emission" vehicles.
     Also, certain materials used to make current batteries and solar cells are
unfriendly to the environment, and their production and eventual disposal
are of concern. Lithium is mostly extracted from salt lakebeds with huge,
ugly processing plants using toxic solvents. Cobalt, used in the energy-dense
NMC batteries, is both poisonous and carcinogenic causing pulmonary,
neurological, and respiratory problems.
     With all things considered, today's electric power cannot compete with
gasoline engines for a "normal" aircraft doing "normal" missions, in terms
742    A i rc raft Design : A C o n c e pt u a l A p p r oa c h


      of attaining a certain speed, range, and payload for a given weight or c o s t
      airplane. At least for now, electric power remains the province of s mall
      UAVs, special-purpose airplanes, nontraditional missions, and fun altern a­
      tives to the conventional approach. The technology is getting bette r,
      though, and the day may soon come when electric airplanes are common.

              E l ectric Motor Basics
            There are many options for aircraft electric propulsion. Electricity can be
        used to power a propeller, or a ducted fan, or even the compressor and/ or fan
       of a fuel-based turbine engine. The wildest concept, studied during the 1960s,
        uses electrohydrodynamic forces (ionic discharge) to accelerate air thro ugh a
       mesh, creating noiseless thrust from a device with no moving parts. Unfortu ­
       nately, the electrical power required to create this thrust is 10-20 tim es
       higher than for a large-diameter propeller. f5 6l
           In most applications the power used for flight comes from an electric
       motor. These are quiet, smooth, and highly reliable. They usually weigh
       less than equivalent power gas motors, even including the motor controller
      normally required.
           The first working direct current (DC) electric motor goes back to 18 27,
      and motors were in commercial production a mere decade later. By 1888,
      electric motors were a proven technology, and the first electric trolleys
      were entering service. That same year eccentric genius Nikola Tesla devel­
      oped a practical alternating current (AC) motor.
           The basic idea of an electric motor consists of a nonmoving magnetic
      object ("stator"), rigged to pull a rotating magnetic object ("rotor") in a circu­
      lar path (Fig. 20. 1). Magnets have north and south poles just like the Earth,
      which actually is a magnet. Opposite poles attract, whereas similar poles
      repel. The rotor and stator have north and south poles on opposite sides o f

                                                  +   -




                                          r-1 �



                                  Fig. 20. 1    Electric motor schematic.
                                                    CHAPTER 20    Electric Aircraft    743


the rotation shaft, so that the rotor is being pulled in the proper direction
fro m both sides .
     After the rotor has been pulled through a path of 180 deg, it would lock to
the position closest to the pulling magnet so that the polarity of the pull is
quickly reversed. The rotor then goes around another 180 deg, and the
p ro cess continues.
     Either the rotor or the stator can be permanent magnets (lodestone or
magn etized metal), or either one can be electromagnets, which are windings
of wire through which a current is passed. At least one of them must be an
electromagnet so that its polarity can be reversed.
     While electric motors are classed as DC or AC by the type of electrical
cu rrent they can accept; inside they are all "alternating current." The
curre nt flow must alternate to reverse magnetic polarity to keep the rotor
spinning around. In a DC motor, the "commutator" switches the polarity
of the current flow to the rotor windings depending on the rotor angle.
Originally this switching was done by mechanical "brushes," which can
literally resemble paint brushes made of wire resting against a rotating elec­
trical contact attached to the rotor. Brushes can also be metallic or graphite
pads that are pressed against the contacts on the rotor. The current flow
direction depends upon which contacts on the rotor are touching the
brushes as it rotates around.
     In modern "brushless" motors, electronic circuits sense the rotor posi­
tion and switch the current flow. This improves efficiency and eliminates
the brushes' high potential for sparking-a very bad thing especially in an
airplane.
     The toy electric motors that we took apart as children are mostly DC,
with permanent magnet stators outside and brushes supplying current to
vary the polarity of the rotating electromagnets inside. This author had
more success taking the111 apart than putting them back together.
     Electric motors for high-power applications more commonly have the
current variation applied to electromagnet stators, with the rotor being
either permanent magnets or electromagnets whose polarity doesn't change.
     Also, practical motors often have the stators inside, with permanent
magnets mounted to a "squirrel cage" rotor in a ring around the fixed
stators. If you take apart that computer in front of you, you'll probably find
this "outrunner" arrangement in its cooling fan.
     Alternating current is just what it sounds like: the current flow constantly
alternates from positive to negative, like household current which alternates
at 50-60 cycles per second (creating the familiar hum when stray current
vibrates hardware or enters sound circuits) . AC current doesn't have to be
phase switched to power an electric motor; it already is. Because the switching
is done by the current itself, the AC motor can normally run only at an rpm
equal to that cycle rate or a submultiple of it. If the rotor is made of electromag­
nets, the current can be passed to it through brushes pressing on concentric
rings. If the rotor uses permanent magnets, brushes are not required.
744     A i rcraft D e s i g n : A C o n c eptu a l A p p ro a c h


               There is a problem with the "two-phase" motor described above, wher e
          the rotor gets pulled through a path of 180 deg and then the polarity is
          reversed. If the rotor is lined up so that the rotor magnet poles are clo sest
          to the stator magnet poles, the magnetic pull is lined up with the axis o f
          rotation so that there is no moment arm, thus no moment, thus no rotatio n .
          The rotor is stuck. Also, the moment arm approaches zero when the rotor
          poles approach the stator poles, so the torque drops towards zero twice in
         each revolution.
              To avoid these problems, the "three-phase" motor was invented (1 890) in
         which additional electromagnets are located around the circumference,
         rigged to switch on and off appropriately to pull only when the geometry
         gives a good moment arm. To make this happen, the alternating current
         itself has three oscillating sinusoidal waves, superimposed and trans mitted
         on the same wires.
              Some electric motors have even more phases, giving better geometry and
         smoother operation at the expense of additional complexity. These can have
         so many different electromagnet locations that the rotor is pulled in its cir­
         cular path by a magnetic attraction circling around like the fake rabbit that
         dashes around a dog race track, keeping just ahead of the dogs.
             A few points relevant to aircraft design: permanent magnet motors are
        more efficient than coil (electromagnet) motors. Alternating current
        motors require AC power whereas batteries and solar cells are direct
        current, so a converter of some sort is required (usually as a part of a
        motor controller) . Motors using brushes are typically less efficient, and the
        likely sparking of brushes is a concern especially with hydrogen fuel cells.
        Brushless motors are usually more efficient and reliable, but need sophisti­
       cated controllers to electronically switch the current at the appropriate
       time so they cost a bit more.
             Brushless DC permanent magnet motors (BLDC-PM) are probably the
       best choice for aircraft applications given their better efficiency and weight,
       lack of sparking, and good torque characteristics. Their reliability and
       safety are likely to be better because the rotating part does not have delicate
       wires. They are used on the Pipistrel Taurus G4, winner of the NASA Green
       Flight Challenge, on the manned electric helicopter, and even on the
       self-balancing Segway Scooter.
            Electric motors always need a "controller" of some sort. This can range
      from an on-off switch to a sophisticated-and expensive-piece of computer­
      driven high-power circuitry. Even an on-off switch will probably need
      overload protection and some scheme for starting the motor at a reduced
      voltage. Over-temperature sensing and shutoff is always a good idea.
            If the power supply is DC as for batteries, the controller will include a
      DC-AC inverter to produce the final current sent to the motor's electromag­
      nets. For this reason, controllers are sometimes referred to as "inverters." By
      adjusting the length of time that current is provided during each rotation, the
      speed and power of the motor is controlled.
                                                 C HA PT E R 20   Electric A i rc raft   745

    A more-sophisticated motor controller allows motor rotation to be
reverse d, or the motor can be convinced to work as a generator when
sl owing down or descending. This is equivalent to putting gasoline back
into the tank when going downhill-a nice trick!
    Such motor controllers are not cheap. They add 15-35% to the motor's
weight, and typically lose about 2% of the electrical energy as waste heat.
Thes e numbers are improving rapidly. An ongoing NASA research project
has inverter/ controller goals of 12 kW/kg with 99% efficiency.

� Power Supply: Batteries
    Electric motors are reliable and lightweight. The only problem is that they
need electrical power, and all of the options weigh a lot more than a tank of
gasoline. For the ion discharge test vehicle described above, the power supply
was a long extension cord. More practical power supplies include batteries,
fuel cells, solar cells, beamed energy, flywheels, or even a conventional
engine coupled to an electrical generator, much like a diesel-electric train.
    All have problems, and all suffer from relatively poor energy density. In
other words, they weigh a lot for the power they can supply over a given
amount of time. Hope for a fivefold breakthrough in stored energy
density-it would change the world.
    Most electric airplanes fly using batteries. The word "battery" actually
comes from none other than Ben Franklin, who was internationally famous
as a leading electrical experimenter long before his involvement in the Amer­
ican Revolution. Around 1750, he was experimenting with Leyden jars, a
recently invented way to store static electricity and a forerunner of today's
capacitors and batteries. To increase total charge-holding ability, he con­
nected a number of them together. When discharged by completing the
circuit (often through al! unsuspecting turkey [5 7l ), the Leyden jars would
make a loud explosive noise, almost but not quite simultaneously, which
Franklin compared to the sound of an artillery battery of cannons. It was
also Franklin who identified and named the positive and negative charges. l58l
    "Cell" is the proper terminology for a single unit that creates electricity
from a chemical reaction. It has three parts: two electrodes, positive and
negative and usually made of dissimilar metals, and the "electrolyte" which
is a chemical surrounding and separating them. The electrolyte can be
liquid or "dry" (actually a paste). Strictly speaking, a "battery" is composed
of one or more such "cells," but we commonly use the terms interchangeably.
When the circuit is completed, ions (positively charged atoms) flow through
the electrolyte one way, while electrons (negatively charged) flow out of the
battery the other way, through the external circuit, and back to the other side
of the battery.
    Franklin's experiments, like all others at that time, were done with static
electricity produced by rubbing things together such as glass rubbed with
one's own hands, or wool rubbed on amber. In 1 800, Alessandro Volta
746   A i r c ra ft Desi g n : A C o n c e p t u a l A p p r o a c h


       invented the "artificial electric organ," a stack of alternating silver and zinc
      disks with saltwater-soaked cloth between them. Each pair of disks, separate d
      by this simple electrolyte, made a cell, and the stack of them made a battery.
      The taller the stack, the more powerful the battery (more "volts," we now say) .
      And unlike the Leyden jars that discharged instantaneously, these batterie s
      could produce a steady current flow.
          Soon renamed the "Voltaic Pile," it became the favorite tool of elec tri cal
      experimenters who discovered they could use it to amuse audiences, kill
      animals, explode gunpowder, and even separate water into oxygen and
      hydrogen. It was the popular fascination with applying electricity to recently
      dead animals that lead Mary Shelley to write her reanimation classic
      Frankenstein.
          Today's batteries are vastly improved over Volta's. For one thing, Volta's
      batteries consumed their electrodes in the chemical reaction so that they
      were not rechargeable. Other than the AA-powered Oxyride describ ed
     above, the batteries used today for aircraft are rechargeable (also called "sec­
     ondary" batteries). Modern batteries have a vastly improved energy density,
     and their power stays relatively constant as the cells are discharged.
         Yet still, we need significant improvement before battery-electric air­
     planes can become truly competitive with fuel-based airplanes. Even after
     the superior efficiency of electric motors is included, gasoline has 20 times
     better effective energy density than the best batteries. f59]
         The classic nickel-cadmium (NiCd, or "NiCad") rechargeable battery,
    invented in Sweden in 1899, is now considered undesirable because the
    cadmium is toxic. They've been superseded by nickel-metal hydride
    (NiMH) batteries, which have slightly better energy density.
        "Li-ion" is a catch-all phrase for a number of different lithium-based
    batteries, each using lithium plus other materials such as cobalt, manganese,
    or nickel. Lithium-ion batteries are common in consumer electronics and are
    currently the only batteries that are really practical for aircraft, automobiles,
    and other vehicle applications. They have better energy density than nickel­
    based batteries and hold their charge for a long time, but present a fire hazard
   especially if they are shorted or charged too rapidly.
        Lithium polymer (LiPO) batteries are simply Li-ion batteries where the
   electrolyte is contained in a solid polymer composite. This makes them
   lighter, and they can be formed into odd shapes. They have the best energy
   density of the readily available batteries for aircraft applications, weighing
   about 1 1 lb {5 kg} per kilowatt-hour produced. They are also more rugged
  and reliable and can discharge at a high power level. Widely used in cell
  phones and model cars, planes, and helicopters, they are prone to explosion
  if short-circuited and to fire if punctured.
       NMC batteries, a type of Li-ion battery using lithium plus nickel, manga­
  nese, and cobalt (oxide) are widely used for automobiles, electric ground
  vehicles, and high-end power tools. These have pretty good specific energy
  and overall performance for an "off the shelf' power supply. They we re
                                                   C H A PT E R 20   Electric Ai rcraft   747


  used by Solar Impulse 2 for its round-the-world flight, to store the day's solar
  en ergy to allow flight throughout the night. Unfortunately, they overheated
  du ring the record-setting Japan to Hawaii leg, grounding the airplane until
  new ones could be installed.
       Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries show promise for the future. These are
  rel atively lightweight and have higher energy density than typical Li-ion
  b atte ries. Li-S batteries were used on the Boeing "Solar Eagle,'' a 400-ft
  {12 2 -m} span UAV designed to fly at high altitudes for a period of five years.
       Silver-zinc batteries have high energy density and are used in torpedoes
 a launch vehicles. Silver-zinc batteries are expensive-check the ingredi­
   nd
 ents list! Also, current versions don't survive many recharging cycles, but
 they have potential for the future.
       Zinc-air batteries are actually not rechargeable, but they are of great
 interest because they are fairly inexpensive and have high energy density
 both by weight and by volume. They work by reacting zinc with atmospheric
 oxygen, essentially "breathing" to make electricity rather than using only
 chemicals contained within themselves. This makes them relatively denser
 in energy terms. While they cannot be recharged by the simple application
 of current, they can be quickly refurbished by physically removing the
 spent zinc oxide and replacing it with fresh zinc. In some concepts this is
 done continuously, making them similar to fuel cells.
       Similarly, aluminum-air batteries offer great promise despite being
 "primary" batteries, i.e. non-rechargeable. After each use they have to be
 refurbished by replacing the corroded aluminum cathode and removing
 the hydrated alumina residue. Clever design could make this a simple flight­
line operation, not much worse than topping off the oil of a piston engine.
      Aluminum-air batteries offer incredible specific energy, up to 8,000 Wh/
 kg theoretically and as much as 1,300 Wh/kg in a "practical" application.
Whether this includes th_e full weight of casing and required support equip­
ment is unclear at this time.
      Startup company Eviation is developing a more-attainable 400 Wh/kg
proprietary system combining lithium-ion for high power operations and
an aluminum-air system for cruise and endurance. Their "Alice" design
concept is a 9-passenger commuter aircraft resembling the old Learfan,
with V-tails, a pusher-prop at the back of the fuselage, and pusher electric
motors at the wingtips. All three motors are the 260 kW Siemens unit
mentioned above. For the initial production version, conventional
lithium-ion batteries of 220 Wh/kg are expected to provide a range of
540 nm with reserves.

 internal electrical components, and other hardware required to turn a labora­
 tory test specimen into a physical battery that you can pick up and place into

      These approximate table values should not be exclusively relied upon
 fo r selection of battery type. You must also consider how many recharge
 cycles the battery can endure, the recharge rate (often 2-3 times slower
th an the discharge rate), temperature sensitivity, insulation and cooling
requirements, fire hazard, system cost, handling issues, and the total
system environmental issues from mining the exotic metals to production
to eventual disposal.
      The safety issues with batteries are always of concern. The more energy
we can pack into a battery of a certain weight and volume, the more it
re se mbles a bomb should all that energy be released at once!
      We know how to prevent that from happening. Like all parts put into an
aircraft, the batteries must be properly constructed including excellent
quality control and testing. Only credible and competent vendors should
be used, and cheap "pirate" parts shouJd be ruthlessly avoided. A sophisti­
cated battery management system (BMS) must be used which monitors the
batteries as to temperature during flight and during charging. Batteries
should be charged at about 5-35 degC. Of course, the system design and
physical installation must prevent shorting across the terminals during
flight or ground handling. Remember the Apollo fire!

r:J Power Supply: Fuel Cells
    Fuel cells are an attractive alternative to batteries for electric aircraft.
They have high energy density and are a well-proven technology. Even
more important, they can be quickly "recharged" by replacing the fuel as
compared to a battery in which one hour of flight time may require three
hours of recharging befo re the next flight.
    Fuel cells work by taking in a slow steady flow of a chemical and reacting
it with an oxidizer, producing electricity as a byproduct. While natural gas
and alcohols can be used, the normal fuel chemical is hydrogen, and the
usual oxidizer is, in fact, atmospheric oxygen. The "exhaust" is then water.
Hydrogen fuel cells have higher energy density than the best batteries and
are roughly twice as efficient as an internal combustion engine. They are
commonly used for spacecraft such as the Space Shuttle and have been
flown in a number of manned and unmanned aircraft. Automobile compa­
nies are investing literally billions of dollars in fuel-cell car development
and expect to enter production in the next decade.
    Hydrogen is bulky unless stored under extreme pressure, making for
heavy tanks. Unlike rechargeable batteries, you must purchase and pump
the hydrogen. This is not currently available at most airports. Also, there is
a lot of waste heat resulting in cooling air intakes about as large as for an
equivalent piston engine airplane. Hydrogen is explosive and flammable, so
750    A i rcraft D e s i g n : A C o n ceptu a l Approach




                            Fig. 20.2   Fuel-cell electric airplane powerplant.

      there is some extra risk from leaks and during crashes. Luckily, when freed it
      rises straight up rather than forming a flaming pool like petroleum fuels.
          There are several types of fuel cells including hydrogen proton exchange
      membrane (PEM), solid-oxide (SOFC), and the older alkaline fuel cell. Details
      are beyond the scope of this book, and the technology is rapidly improvin g.
          Figure 20.2 shows the powerplant of a fuel cell-electric airplane seen at
      the EAA AirVenture airshow and fly-in. The fuel cells are tucked underneath,
      to the right. The hydrogen tank is located behind the cabin, and surge battery
      banks are in the wing leading edge. Note that the motor controller is big­
      about the size of the actual motor (on the left, attached to the propeller).

             Power Supply: Hybrid-Electric
          Hybrid-electric power goes back to the 1930's when trains and submar­
      ines began using electric motors powered by diesel engines driving electrical
      generators. In some cases, the diesel engine could also directly drive the
      vehicle to avoid the conversion inefficiencies, but for simplicity sake most
      of these vehicles used only the electric motors for the final drivetrain.
          For diesel-electric trains, still ubiquitous today, this hybrid power plant
      avoids the need for clutches and gearing, and provides smooth torque in
      all conditions. When submerged, hybrid power allows submarines to be
      powered by batteries which are charged by the diesel engine while cruising
      on the surface.
          The hybrid-electric concept has a special benefit when applied to auto­
      mobiles. Cars must accelerate quickly and occasionally climb steep hills,
                                                  C H A P T E R 20   Electric Aircraft   75 1


 but most of the time they need far less power. The fueled (gasoline) engine
 ca n be made smaller, being sized only for continuous cruising power
 ne eds. Battery power is used for surge needs. Better yet, the fueled engine
 ca n be shut off when the battery has enough charge to meet the current
 p ower needs, or when the car is stopped in traffic. This greatly increases
 overall fuel efficiency. Some hybrid cars even allow charging overnight
 through the ground power grid. If you don't travel long distances, you
 might go six months without refilling the gas tank.
      Hybrid power might be the perfect power supply for electric airplanes,
 ble nding the smoothness and reliability of an electric motor with the high
 en ergy content of a tank of gasoline. There are many options. The fueled
 engine can be piston or turbine, and the fuel can be gasoline, diesel, kerosene,
 methane, hydrogen, or others. Most hybrid concepts use batteries for energy
 storage and management, but they aren't required.
     There are several options for the drive train. A propeller or ducted fan can
 be driven solely by the electric motor, as in the submarines, trains, and auto­
 mobiles described above. This is called. "series hybrid" or in the automotive
 wo rld, "extended-range electric vehicles (EREV)." In effect, the generator
 and electric motor replace the transmission of a conventionally-fueled
 engine, then batteries are added for additional capabilities.
     This approach takes advantage of the smoothness of an electric motor
and allows the propeller or fan to be located away from the fueled engine.
 If the batteries are big enough, the aircraft can take off on battery power
 alone with benefits to noise and local pollution, or even fly for shorter mis­
 sions without ever starting the fueled engine.
     Unfortunately, there is an efficiency loss of 10- 15% when the shaft power
 of the fueled engine is converted to electricity via a generator, and then back
into shaft power by an electric motor. All this equipment weighs a lot more
than the handful of bolts used to directly attach a propeller to a conventional
engine. It adds to the vol u me inside the aircraft as well, leading to increased
wetted area and airframe structural weight.
     On the other hand, perhaps the heavy flywheel built into a piston engine
can be eliminated if the attached generator can serve the same damping func­
tion. Perhaps the generator can "work backwards" and serve as the starter
motor. The propeller itself may be lighter if it doesn't have to be attached
to a jerky internal combustion engine. With these savings and the inherently
smaller fueled engine, there may be no net penalty or even a weight savings.
     Another drive train option is to use the electric motor as a "booster" for
the fueled engine. The propeller is directly attached to the fueled engine as for
a normal aircraft, with an electric motor either geared in (with clutch) or lit­
erally wrapped around the output shaft. The electric motor is also a genera­
tor, so it can be used to store energy in batteries when power demands are
low, and can be used to add horsepower during takeoff and initial climb.
Perhaps the batteries can be ground-charged before takeoff for an additional
boost.
752    A i rc raft Desi g n : A Concept u a l Approach

             The main benefit of this "booster" approach is that it allows a s mall er
        fueled engine (and thus, lighter and cheaper) . That smaller engin e can b e
        better matched to the lower power demands during cruise. The elec tric
        motor is also smaller than for the other hybrid concept since it does n ' t
        have to power the aircraft all by itself. Note that this hybrid app roach
        doesn't allow takeoff or flight on electric power alone.
             This "booster" approach is actually a variant of the "parallel hybrid"
        arrangement, in which the fueled or the electric motor can each drive th e
        vehicle separately, or they can work together. This is used for sever al
        hybrid automobiles. For an aircraft this would require additional clutching,
        to disconnect the propeller from the fueled engine during electric-only flight.
             Yet another option, similar to the automotive "through-the-road
        (TTR)" hybrid, would have a conventional fueled engine with a dedicated
        propeller, and a completely separate electric motor with its own propeller.
        The aircraft could be flown on either propulsion system alone, or using
        both when maximum thrust is required. Probably the fueled engine
       would be attached to a generator to charge up the batteries for the ele ctric
       motor. Clever design would be required to avoid large stopped-prop drag
       penalties.
             Some have proposed such a "through-the-air" hybrid arrangement using
       small electric motors on the wingtips in a pusher configuration. These would
       get extra thrust by "unwrapping" the rotation of the wingtip vortex. Unfortu­
       nately, the prop blades would cut through the wing wake causing vibration,
       noise, and loss of efficiency. Still, it may be a useful approach both for hybrid
       designs and for all-electric aircraft.
            There are several significant projects in work to develop hybrid-electric
       commercial airliners. The regional aircraft market makes a logical application
      for hybrid-electric power. Although a ducted fan might look like a jet engine,
       it's really a propeller with a ring around it. These are more efficient at lower
      speeds and for shorter distances, but not for long range flight at near­
      transonic speeds.
            With backing from Boeing, startup firm Zunum Aero is developing a
      12-seat commercial hybrid-electric aircraft and has plans for designs of up
      to 50 seats. The Zuma concept is essentially a battery-powered electric
      fan aircraft much like hobby model airplanes, but with a 670 hp {500 kw}
      turboshaft engine buried in the fuselage for range extension. For takeoff
      and shorter missions the wing-mounted batteries, charged on the ground
      and quickly replaceable, are sufficient.
            The 12-seat Zunum design will weigh about 12,500 lbs {5670 kg} and
      have a range of over 600 nmi { 1, 126 km} with a cruise speed of 300 kts
      {550 kph}. Cost is projected to be 8 cents per seat mile, versus around 25
      for current commuter aircraft.
            Airbus, in association with Rolls-Royce and Siemens, will flight-test a
      modified BAe 146 commuter aircraft with one of its four turbofans replaced
      with a 2700 hp {2,000 kw} electric motor driving a ducted fan. They plan to
                                                        C H APTE R 20   Electric Ai rcraft   753


ap ply hybrid-electric propulsion to future regional airliners of up to 100
p assengers.
    The recent EU HYPSTAIR project has demonstrated an advanced
hybrid- electric power system suitable for high-performance GA aircraft.
The Siemens-developed 270 hp {200 kw} hybrid propulsion system, based
o n a Rotax 914, was installed and ground-tested in a modified Pipistrel
Panthera airframe. The generator exceeds 95% efficiency and only weighs
abo ut 7 kW/kg. The electric motor was attached to an efficient five-bladed,
low- rpm propeller. Production of this exact design is not expected, but
similar projects are in work.

     Power Supply: Solar Cel ls
      Another type of electrical power supply increasingly used for aircraft
applications is the solar cell. These are panels that convert sunlight to elec­
tricity by the photovoltaic effect, first discovered in 1 839 and resulting in a
working solar cell by 1883. Modern solar cells were introduced in 1 954
and are related to transistors, being solid-state semiconductor devices and
u sually made of crystalline silicon. While solar cells were hideously expensive
j u st a few years ago, today they cost as little as a dollar per watt of solar-cell
capability. The integration and control system costs add a similar amount.
      Solar cells are well-proven for flight applications. They're just expensive
and heavy. The first flight by solar cell alone was a large model airplane in
1974 called "Sunrise I." Funded by DARPA, it flew for about 20 miles.
      The manned Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar cells. It used
solar cells by day and lithium polymer batteries by night, with sufficient
excess power to charge the batteries while flying during the day. The airplane
is huge, with a wingspan of 236 ft {7 1 .9 m}. The round-the-world trip took 23
days and nights of flight ttme, spread out over many months due to technical
and weather issues. (The similar Solar Impulse 1 is shown in Fig. 20.3.)




                           I !




      Fig. 20.3   Solar Impulse (© Solar Impulse/Fred Merz, used with permission).
  7 54    A i rcraft Des i g n : A C o n ceptu a l A p p ro a c h


                  Ideally, solar cells should attain about 0. 1 kW of power per squa re fo ot
           { 1 . 1 kW/m2 }, but we are far from that. Current efficiencies give abo ut
           0.02 kW/ft2 {0.2 1 kW/m 2 }, so it takes almost 40 ft2 to obtain 1 hp in equ iv­
           alent electricity {"-'5 m2 to give 1 kW}. They typically weigh about 0. 06 p sf
           {0.3 kg/m 2 }. Efficiencies are improving rapidly, so don't use these valu es
           for your design. Note that solar cells don't age well, losing over 1 % effici ency
           per year when in service.
                  There is a substantial installation weight for solar cells, almost do ubling
           the cell weight. Also, they are not formed to the desired airfoil contour, so
           they can affect the airflow and make it difficult to maintain lamin ar flow.
           Solar cells printed on flexible plastic sheet are in development and offer
          both reduced weight and smoother airfoil contours.
                  When calculating the power obtained from solar cells, don't forget the
          time of day! Maximum power is obtained only at "high noon." There is a sinu­
          soidal drop-off during the other daylight hours, and, of course, no power at
          night. The climate and latitude of flight also matter, along with the obvious
          time of year. Atmospheric vapor affects the amount of power obtained.
          Flight in northern Sweden in late December won't be as easy as flight over
          southern Somalia.
                 Pointing must be considered. The solar power depends upon the
          projected area of the cells, measured in the direction of the sun (sine func­
          tion) . For that flight in northern Sweden, or for flight just after dawn or
         just before dusk, the top of the wings is a bad location for the solar cells.
         Some solar-powered airplanes have added non-lifting solar cell panels that
         can be aimed at the sun, or even wings that buckle into a sawtooth shape
         when seen from the front.
                 There is an altitude effect as well, with high altitudes generally being
         favorable. There is less air to filter out the sunlight, less moisture in the
         air, and less concern about clouds. There is no concern if you are high
         enough! This amounts to roughly 30% more available solar power outside
         the atmosphere vs at sea level.
                 Lecture notes [60] by Noth, Siegwart, and Engel detail the design of solar­
         powered aircraft including solar irradiance estimation and statistically
         derived parameters needed for sizing of both aircraft and solar cells. The
         technology is improving rapidly, and current data for various efficiencies
         and other parameters can be found online and from company sources.

- 20. 9         Power Supply: Beamed Power
             A big problem for solar cells is the sun-it is often uncooperative, appear­
         ing at neither the time nor the place where we wish it to be. What if we made
         our own? Nikola Tesla, inventor of the AC motor, suggested powering elec­
         tric airplanes by beams from the ground.
             This might be an ideal solution for a perpetual endurance unmanned air­
         craft designed to circle over a city, providing cell-phone relay, television
                                                                CHAPTE R 20      Electric Airc raft     755


   transmission, police and firefighter surveillance, and other urban services.
   p0wer could be beamed as visible light and absorbed by solar cells on the
  bo tto m of the aircraft, but microwave transmission offers better efficiency.
        In 1964, Raytheon demonstrated this concept by beaming microwave
  p ower from the ground to a hovering helicopter where it was collected by
  a rectifying antenna and converted into electrical power. In 1987, a project
  funded by the Communications Research Centre of Canada demonstrated
  fl ight powered by beamed microwave energy. This 15-ft {4.5-m} span
  unmanned aircraft took off on battery power but switched to beamed
  power and flew for over an hour. In a scaled-up version there would be suffi­
  cient beamed power to operate onboard communication equipment, acting
  as a "poor man's" satellite.
       The obvious problem: what if birds or other airplanes fly through the
 beam? Some sort of automatic shutoff is probably required for these transi­
 tory events. Also, power reception is limited to line-of-sight of the ground
 transmitting station.
       Still, it is an interesting concept and_ probably better than the use of solar
 cells for such applications. Solar cells can barely fly the airplane. There simply
 isn't enough solar energy available to also power the onboard mission equip­
 ment such as cell-phone relay transmitters, especially at night! Tesla's
 beamed energy just might be the answer.

[1 E lectric Aircraft I n itial Sizing
    Previous chapters introduced "Sizing" as the process which calculates
how big and heavy the as-yet-undrawn aircraft must be to attain the required
mission range carrying the design payload. The methods used for fuel­
burning engines begin with an indirect estimation of the fuel burn using a
ratio between each mission segment's starting and ending weight, called
the mission segment weight fraction ( Wi / Wi- 1 ). The most important ones
are based on the Breguet range and loiter equations, found by integrating
the vehicle weight change as fuel is burned (Chapter 17). These ratios are
then used in an iterative process to find an aircraft takeoff gross weight at
which there is sufficient fuel weight available to perform the mission.
758    A i rc raft Des i g n : A Conceptual Approach

           For battery-electric aircraft a similar method can be defined bu t the
       Breguet equations are inapplicable. There is no fuel burned, no change in
       weight, and hence no analysis by integration of the change in weight.
       Instead, the required battery mass for each mission segment is devel op ed
       using the equations above, expressed as the ratio (mb /m). This can be
       called Battery Mass Fraction, or EMF.
           Battery Mass Fraction is the ratio of battery mass to all-up aircraft mass
       (or weight). The EMF values calculated for the various mission segments are
       used in an iterative process described below in which the fraction of total air ­
       craft mass available for batteries is compared to the battery mass fractio n
       required to do the mission.
           EMF has a "talking" resemblance to the Propellant Mass Fraction used in
       rocket analysis. Like PMF, a high value of EMF is required to obtain goo d
      range and performance but can only be assured if the vehicle empty weight
      is kept low.
           Compared to the fuel-burning aircraft analysis of Chapters 3 and 6,
      EMF is analogous to a value of one minus the mission segment weight
      fraction (1 - Wi/ Wi - 1 ) . However, methods developed for fuel-burning air­
      craft should not be applied to electric aircraft because their derivations
      assumed that the aircraft gets lighter as the mission segment progresses.
      Instead, we start with the electric aircraft equations found in the previous
      section.

      found by solving the equation Eq. (20. 1), substituting mg(P/ W) for P:

            Despite a different derivation, this is nearly identical to the preliminary
       sizing equation presented in Chapter 3 (Eq. 3.4), with EMF as somehow
       equivalent to fuel fraction. Selecting a specific value for empty weight fraction
       makes this a closed-form calculation, but this is a simplistic assumption.
            The empty weight fraction for initial sizing is better estimated from a stat­
       istical logarithmic relationship based on gross weight ( W0), as describe d in
       Chapter 3. An iteration process must then be applied to solve the sizing
       equation. First guess W0, then calculate We/ W0, and then use that and the
       required EMF to calculate W0• Iterate until the calculated value equals the
      guess value.
           Since batteries are here considered equivalent to full fuel tanks, the emp ty
      weight statistical equations of Chapter 3 can be used as a first approximation
      for We/ W0• Those are based on aircraft with fuel-burning engines so it is wise
      to adjust the constant terms using data for recent electric-powered aircraft.
           In this formulation, We includes all empty weight items including propul­
      sion, structure, avionics, and everything else that isn't payload or usable bat­
      teries. This is analogous to the empty weight definition used throughout this
      book, letting batteries take the place of fuel. All of the items in We are
      assumed to vary with W0•
           Alternatively, one could treat propulsion and avionics a s "payload" with
      fixed values, removing them from the estimation of We . Or, portions could
      be split between the two.
           This sizing process is laborious and sometimes too much effort for
      designers of small and simple aircraft. It is fairly common in the design of
      electric-powered aircraft to select a motor as "about right" for the class of air­
      craft, and then find the aircraft weight based on a P/ W estimated for per­
      formance reasons (Eq. 6.24) . The entire sizing process described above is
      skipped, but the mission range isn't know until later calculations are com­
      pleted. If range is not met, a more-powerful motor and a higher gross
      weight must be assumed and the process repeated.

         The first type of vertical takeoff heavier-than-air
    aircraft was the helicopter, which was conceived by Leonardo da Vinci but not
    regularly used until shortly after World War II. The helicopter rapidly proved
    its worth for rescue operations and short-range point-to-point transportation,
    but its inherent speed and range limitations restricted its application.
        For aircraft designers, vertical flight in an otherwise "normal" airplane
    remains an elusive and challenging goal. A clear "best" solution for vertical


                                                                                                              763
    764    A i r c ra ft Des ig n : A C o n c e p t u a l A p p r o a c h


           lift has yet to emerge. For propeller-powered aircraft, the tilt-rotor concept
           has proven to be a good compromise between helicopter-like vertical flight
           and efficient wing-borne cruise. This is the basis of the combat-proven
           V-22 Osprey, but other approaches are still being pursued and might ulti ­
           mately prove superior.
                For jet aircraft, a "best" solution is even more elusive. Instead, there are
           many different vertical-lift concepts, some tested and some not, available
           for incorporation into a new design. Selection of a best concept depends
           upon the intended mission and operational environment as well as the tech­
           nical details of the selected lift concept. Ultimately, system-level trade stu dies
           should be used to select the best approach for a new project. But be suspi­
           cious of the latest innovation-new ideas always weigh more than we think
           they will, and weight is death to vertical takeoff airplanes.

,,..,.. 2 1 .2    Jet VTOL
          #JfJI Introduction
                Vertical-takeoff-and-landing (VTOL) capability was pursued almost as
           soon as the jet was invented. The jet engine's high thrust-to-weight ratio
           seems to lend itself to vertical flight, and both military and commercial cus­
           tomers would be delighted to be able to take off and land without the need for
           long runways.
                To date, there have only been three* operational jet VTOL designs:
           the British Harrier, the Russian YAK 38, and the US F-35B. The first two
           are subsonic aircraft and have limited range. Were it not for their vertical
           flight capability and modern avionics, their overall flight performance
           would place them with aircraft of the mid 1950's.
                A VTOL aircraft with supersonic capabilities is an orders-of-magnitude
           more difficult challenge. Although the VTOL Mirage III-V flew at Mach 2
           back in 1 966, it was not considered practical enough for operational develop­
           ment. Similarly, the Russian YAK- 141 flew at Ml.7 but was cancelled as
          impractical and too expensive. For almost half a
          century after 1966, not a single supersonic VTOL                 Supersonic STOVL:
          aircraft entered service.                                        The Future is Now.
               This is largely because the engine modifications            -D. Raymer,

up to now to provide both vertical flight and supersonic forward flight in an

     Thanks to broad advances in engines, structures, flight control, and
VTO L technology, we can finally say "The Future Is Now!". l13 0l The F-35B

capability. While a huge improvement over the subsonic Harriers it will
replace, it suffers by comparison to the similar but non-VTOL F-35A. The
B has about a third less fuel volume, lost to the vertical flight equipment.
To save empty weight it was redesigned to a lower structural load factor capa­

1,0 00 lb weapons internally versus the 2,000 lb-ers of the A model. It has
no internal gun, unlike the A, and must "strap on" a gun pod for missions
where it may be needed, giving up even more range or payload.
     But for missions where a long runway or a huge aircraft carrier is not an
option, the F-35B is the only option, and it brings stealth, incredible avionics,
and advanced systems to the theater. Nothing else compares.
     As for commercial jet VTOL applications, passenger aircraft that can fly
off a downtown rooftop-that remains for the distant future, if ever.


flfII VTOL Terminology
    VTOL refers to a capability for vertical takeoff and landing, as opposed to
conventional takeoff and landing (CTOL).
    An aircraft that has the flexibility to perform either vertical or short
takeoffs and landings is said to have vertical or short-takeoff-and-landing
(VSTOL) capability. An aircraft that has insufficient lift for vertical flight at
takeoff weight but that can land vertically at landing weight is called short
takeoff-vertical land (STOVL) .
    The "tail-sitter" or vertical-attitude-takeoff-and-landing (VATOL) air­
craft cannot use its vertical lift capability to shorten a conventional takeoff
or landing roll. In contrast, a horizontal-attitude-takeoff-and-land (HATOL)
concept can usually deflect part of its thrust downward while in forward
flight enabling it to perform a short takeoff and landing (STOL).


fJfU Fundamenta l Problems of VTOL Design
    A number of unique problems characterize the design and operation of
jet VTOL aircraft. Two fundamental problems stand out because they tend
to have the greatest impact upon the selection of a VTOL propulsion
concept and upon the design and sizing of the aircraft: balance and thrust
matching.
    Modern supersonic jet fighters have a T/ W exceeding 1 .0, so it would
seem fairly easy to point the jet exhaust downward and attain vertical
flight. Unfortunately, this is complicated by the balance problem.
                     /7

            a) Forward flight                                b) Magic finger vertical flight



           d:-s-c
                ""'="TI.-
                                                                                               t



           c) Thrust location moved




                                      Fig. 2 1 . 1   The balance problem .

             Many subsonic jets and virtually all supersonic jets are designed with the
       engine at the rear, the cockpit and avionics at the nose, and the payload
        and fuel near the center of the aircraft. This traditional layout places the
       expendables on the e.g., collocates the parts of the aircraft requiring
       cooling (crew and avionics), and keeps the avionics away from the hot and
       vibrating engine.
             Figure 2 1 . l a illustrates this traditional (and usually optimal) layout. If the
       aircraft's thrust exceeds its weight, vertical flight could be obtained simply by
       deflecting the thrust downward, as shown in Fig. 2 1 . lb. However, a "magic
       finger" must hold up the nose to balance the vertical thrust force at the
       tail. This balance problem is possibly the single most important driver of
       the design of the VTOL jet fighter.
            There are really only two conceptual approaches to solving the balance
       problem. Either the thrust can somehow be moved to the e.g. (Fig. 21.lc),
       or an additional thrust force can be located near the nose (Fig. 21. ld).
       Both of these approaches will tend to compromise the aircraft away from
      the traditional and usually optimal layout.
            (While Director of Advanced Design at Lockheed, this author had the
      crazy idea to hold up the nose with gyroscopic flywheels, like a child's toy.
      A calculation was made of the needed gyroscopic forces. The required fly­
      wheels were way too heavy. Crazy Raymer.)
           For cruise-dominated VTOL aircraft such as transports, a more severe
      problem involves thrust matching. If the thrust required for vertical flight
      is provided by the same engines used for cruise, the engines will be far too
      large for efficient cruise.
           As an example, imagine designing a VTOL transport using four of the
      TF-39 engines used in the C-5. These produce about 40,000 lb {178 kN} of
      thrust at sea-level static conditions, or 160,000 lb {712 kN} altogether. If
                                      C HAPTE R 2 1   Vertical F l i g ht-Jet and Prop   767


 the aircraft is to have a typical 30% thrust surplus for vertical flight (T/
 W == 1.3), then the aircraft can weigh no more than 123,077 lb {55,827 kg}
 at takeoff. Note that this is far less than the C-5 at 764,000 lb {346,544 kg}.
      Assume a typical cruise L / D of 18 yields a required T/ W during cruise of
 ab o ut 1 / 1 8, or 0.056. If the aircraft weight at the beginning of cruise is about
9 5 % of the takeoff weight, then the total thrust required during cruise is only
6 ,496 lb (123,077 x 0.95 x 0.056) {29 kN}.
      This is only 1,624 lb {7 kN} of thrust per engine, which is about 18% of the
available thrust for that engine at a typical cruise altitude of 35,000 ft
 (1 0,668 m}. It is doubtful that the engine would even run at that low of a
thrust setting.
      At 35,000 ft and Mach 0.9, the best SFC for this engine would be about
0. 73 at a thrust of 9,000 lb {40 kN} per engine. The SFC at the 50% throttle
setting is about 1 .2 {34 mg/Ns}. This is 64% worse than the SFC at the
higher thrust setting. If the engine would run at only 18% of its available
thrust, its SFC would be even worse than the 1 .2 value.
      Aircraft range is directly proportional to SFC. The mismatch between
thrust for vertical flight and thrust for cruise will produce a fuel consumption
and range penalty for a cruise-dominated design that uses only the vectored
thrust of its cruise engines for vertical flight. For this reason, many concep­
tual VTOL transport designs incorporate separate "lift engines" used during
vertical flight.
      If three of the TF-39 engines in the previous example could be turned off
during cruise (without a drag penalty), the remaining engine could be oper­
ated at a 72% thrust setting where it gets an SFC of about 0.8 {23 mg/Ns}.
This is a big improvement over all engines being used for both lift and
cruise. However, the use of separate lift engines introduces additional
problems, as discussed later.
      There are numerous other problems associated with VTOL aircraft
design including transiti � n, control, suckdown, hot gas ingestion, FOD,
inlet flow matching, and ground erosion. These are discussed next following
a brief discussion of the various VTOL jet propulsion options that are
currently available to the designer.

#JfJI VTOL Jet Propulsion Options
    Broadly speaking, jet VTOL concepts can be divided into those that
utilize fairly conventional engines and those that use engines modified so
that the fan and core air are split, with the fan air ducted and exhausted
from some place separate from the core air.
    The conventional-engine VTOL concepts that do not use additional lift
engines for vertical flight must have a net takeoff T/ W in excess of 1 .0.
If the jet exhaust is not diverted to some other location for vertical flight,
the aircraft must either be a tail sitter (VATOL) or have the engine
exh aust at the aircraft e.g. and capable of vectoring downward for vertical
768    A i rc raft Desi g n : A Conceptu a l Approach

        flight. This can be accomplished by using a vectoring nozzle or nacelles that
        tilt (Fig. 2 1 .2).
             The YAK-36 and the X- 14 research aircraft had vectoring nozzles at the
        e.g., with the engines out in front. This is probably not a good arrangement
        for most applications because the cockpit winds up in back, for balanc e, an d
        thus does not provide acceptable visibility for the pilot. Also, in forward flight
       the jet exhaust scrubs alongside the fuselage, causing thermal and aco ustic
       problems.
             An alternative approach is to place the nozzles at the center of gravity and
       put the engine in the rear fuselage as on a regular aircraft, but installed back­
       ward! This RIVET concept offers design simplicity, reduced weight, ease of
       transition, and inherent vectoring in forward flight (VIFF). However, inl et
       duct losses of 5% or more will be caused by the 180-deg bend req uired
       to supply air to a backwards engine. Sizing studies [ 1 30, 142] indic ate
       that, despite these duct losses, RIVET offers a viable option for superson ic
       V/STOL.
            Tilt nacelles, although heavy, might be the best compromise for some
      applications. Grumman pursued a tilt-nacelle concept for naval applicatio n s
      for a number of years, even flying a subscale model.
            Some VTOL concepts provide a means of diverting the exhaust flow to
      gain vertical lift. This is generally done by a retracting blocker device in
      the engine that shuts off the flow through the rearward-facing nozzle. The
      flow is then diverted forward through internal ducting (Fig. 21 .3).




         a) Tail sitter
                                              b) Vectored thrust at e.g.




                                             c) Tilt nacelle at e.g.




                    Fig. 2 1 . 2   Conventional engine, no lift engine, no flow diversion.

          Fig. 2 1 . 3   Conventional engine, no lift engines, flow diversion used .

    The diverted flow can be exhausted directly downwards, or it can be "aug­
mented" by either a gas- driven fan or an ejector. Both of these can increase
the thrust obtained from the diverted flow by using the energy of the
exhaust flow to accelerate a larger mass of air. This augments thrust by
increasing the propulsive efficiency, as explained by Eq, (13.4) ,
    The gas-driven fan is a ducted fan that is turned by turbine blades spun
by diverted engine exhaust or sometimes, diverted compressor air. The gas­
driven fan's turbine blades can be inside the fan or out at the tips of the fan
blades, in which case it is sometimes called a tip-driven fan.
    The Ryan XV-SA used tip-driven fans and attained an "augmentation
ratio" of almost three, that is, the lifting thrust attained with the tip-driven
fans was almost three times the thrust produced by the jet engines alone.
This is probably the highest augmentation ratio ever obtained for a jet
VTOL design. The XV-SA was being considered for rescue operations
where its combination of high forward speed and hover capability would
be beneficial, but during tests, the dummy being winched into the airplane
was somehow blown to the top of the wing and sucked into the tip-driven fan.
770      A i rcraft D e s i g n : A Conceptu a l A p p roach


                 The ejector makes use of the viscosity of the air. Any exhaust j et will
            "drag" along adjacent air molecules, accelerating the free air in its vicinity.
            The ejector consists of a short duct with an exhaust stream blowing down
            it. Additional air is pulled by viscosity into the duct, accelerated, and
            ejected through a nozzle. This produces thrust greater than the thrus t due
           to the jet exhaust alone.
                While ejectors promise theoretical augmentation ratios of 3 or more, a
           more realistic value ranges from about 1 .3 to perhaps 2.2. The Roc kwell
           XFV- 12A featured ejectors along the entire span of the wing and canard.
           It was expected to produce a high value of augmentation ratio. The actual
           value achieved was only about 1 .5, and it never flew.
                Both ejectors and gas-driven fans are heavy and tend to chop up the aircraft
           structure. Also, the internal ducting is bulky and poses a thermal problem.
          However, ejectors and gas-driven fans tend to reduce the thrust-matching
          problem because the engines do not have to be sized to lift the aircraft by jet
          thrust alone. The resulting improvement in cruise fuel consumption can
          offset the weight of the ejector or gas-driven fan (but probably not).
                One of the simplest ways of providing VTOL capability is to add lift engines
          to an essentially conventional aircraft (Fig. 21.4). This brute-force approach
         was used in the Mirage III-V. Obviously, the separate lift engines add consider­
         able weight and volume to the design, but the forward-flight engine can be
         sized for efficient cruise, thus solving the thrust-matching problem.
               Because the lift engines are designed for a single operating condition,
         they can be highly optimized for that condition. Existing lift engines have
         uninstalled engine T/ W on the order of 15, compared to about 6-8 for
         a typical forward-flight engine. Future lift engines are expected to have
         engine T/ W of 25 or more. Installation including doors and a vectoring lift
        nozzle will roughly double the weight.
               The lift-engines-only approach seems rather silly. The airplane has a
        large jet engine for forward flight, but it is turned off for takeoff. If the forward­
        flight engine is fitted with some means for vectoring its thrust downward for
       takeoff, then the lift engines can be fewer or smaller. For balance reasons, the
        lift engines will be placed forward, probably just behind the cockpit. This is
       known as "lift plus lift / cruise" (L + L / C) and was used on the operational
       YAK-38 and the supersonic but ultimately unsuccessful YAK- 141 .
              Numerous studies going back many years have identified L + L / C as a
       good and maybe the best approach for supersonic VTOL. It uses the lift of
       the main engine plus the extra lift of the lift engines (one or more), in a
       design that is not compromised away from a "normal" aircraft configuration.
      George Spangenberg, legendary director of Naval Air Systems Command's
      Evaluation Division, wrote, "If a supersonic V/STOL fighter capability is
      required, it is probable that the lift plus lift cruise configuration is still the
      most promising."
             A problem with L + L / C: If a lift engine should fail during vertical
      flight or transition, the aircraft would instantly pitch nose down. The
                                                  C HA P T E R 2 1   Vertical F l i g ht-Jet a n d Prop   771


          a) Sepa rate l ift e n g i n es




                                                       I       I
          b) L + L/C (vectored)




                                                  J
          c) L + L/C (tilt nacelle)




                       C::J
          c:::::                                LI         •


                                                  �                     �
                       Fig. 2 1 .4          Conventional engine with lift engines.


Yakovlev designs have an automatic ejection seat to save the pilot in this
event. To be fair, engine failure in any jet VTOL design requires immediate
ejection.
    During transition from hover to forward flight, the lift/cruise engine's
thrust is being vectored rearward, decreasing the vertical component of
thrust. Because the lift/ cruise engine is at the back of the aircraft, there
might be a nose-up pitching moment. Probably vectoring should be added
to the lift engine to improve transition.
    If rearward vectoring is added to the lift engine, its thrust can be used to
return to base in the event that the cruise engine fails. No other VTOL
approach allows this.
    Perhaps the main problem with L + L/C is that the aircraft operators
would rather not have to provide maintenance and support for two types of
engines in one aircraft. This was considered a serious disadvantage in the
early downselect for the JSF /F-35 program. However, any choice should be
based on the maintenance of the total system, and all VTOL concepts have
problems in this area.

           The "shaft-driven lift fan" (SDLF) is basically L + L/C, but the fron t lift
       engine is replaced with a "fan," which is really more like a jet engine co mp re s­
       sor than a shrouded propeller. This is mechanically spun by a driveshaft th at
       is powered by an extra turbine in the engine exhaust. For horizontal flight the
       fan drive is declutched, and the now-unloaded turbine spins freely.
                                                                      i o
      Figure 2 1 .5 shows an early Lockheed SDLF concept [ 3 ] with ste alth
      shaping, and of course, today's F-35B uses SDLF.
           SDLF has many of the benefits of L + L/C but avoids the higher tempera­
      tures and maintenance of a separate lift engine. However, the shaft, clutch,
      gearbox, extra turbine, and the fan all add to the maintenance, which must
      be included in a system-level comparison to the other options for jet
      VTOL. Also, the return-to-base capability of L + L/C is lost.
           When the fan is engaged, mechanical power is extracted from the engine
      exhaust and applied to a larger amount of air, augmenting the thrust as
      explained by Eq. (1 3.4) . Available F-35B data indicate a 1 .4 augmentation
      factor, but this augmentation produces less total lift than would be obtained
      by a same-size lift engine.

    Interestingly, SDLF is slightly related to a 1956 design called the "Gyro­
ptere," which had four lift fans mechanically powered by a shaft coming
from a turbine engine. These rotated rearward for forward flight, but the
design, never built, was found to be clumsy and heavy. Its concept of four­
post vectored thrust actually inspired the invention of the Pegasus engine
used in the Harrier, described next.
    A number of VTOL propulsion concepts are based upon a "split-flow"
modification to the turbofan engine. The airflow from the fan is split away
from the core airflow and used in some fashion to address the balance
and/or thrust-matching pr9blems.
    One such approach exhausts the fan air separately and provides a means
for vectoring it downward for vertical flight (Fig. 21 .6a). The AV-8 Harrier
uses the high-bypass Pegasus engine in which the fan air and core air are
each separately vectored through "elbow" nozzles (described later) . This
permits nearly instantaneous vectoring of thrust with no mode changes
(such as starting a lift engine or diverting air into an ejector). This approach
also simplifies transition and enhances maneuverability.
    On the negative side, the Pegasus-type engine suffers the thrust-matching
problem because the engine thrust must provide all of the required lifting
force. Also, the engine must straddle the aircraft e.g. This increases the
aircraft's cross-sectional area right at the wing location and thus increases
supersonic wave drag. The successful Harrier is subsonic so this isn't a
problem. Despite years of design studies, no viable supersonic configuration
bas ed on the split-flow approach was ever found.
    It is possible to augment the thrust of such an engine by essentially provid­
ing an "afterburner" for the fan and core airflows in so-called plenum-chamber
774   A i rcraft Desi g n : A C o n c e ptu a l A p p r o a c h


       burning (PCB). The desirability of such high-temperature exhaust passing next
       to the aircraft skins or blowing down on the landing site is debatable.
           Another means of providing afterburning to the Pegasus-type split flow
       engine is to change it to a conventional engine for forward flight, shu tti ng
       off the side nozzles and ducting both fan and core air together. Then a co n­
       ventional afterburner can be added. However, this requires that the engine be
       sized for vertical flight without afterburning, leading to penalties in fuel effi­
       ciency, weight, and cost.
           A close relative of the vectored-thrust split-flow engine is the tandem fan
       (Fig. 21 .6b), a dual-cycle engine that features an additional fan ahead of the
       regular one. During forward flight, the front fan acts to "supercharge" the
      rear fan and engine core.
           For vertical flight the flow from the front fan is diverted by blocker doors
      and exits from a downward-facing front nozzle. Auxiliary doors open to
      provide air to the rear fan and engine core. This has the effect of increasing
      the total amount of air that the engine acts upon and therefore increasing the
      thrust efficiency.
           The tandem fan is fairly heavy compared to a normal engine, but does
      provide a clever means of augmenting the vertical lift and of moving the
      center of vertical lift forward. The tandem fan engine has a much higher
      effective bypass ratio when operating in vertical than in forward flight. A
      modified version of the tandem fan called the hybrid fan (Fig. 21.6c)
      permits the high-bypass mode to be used in forward flight.
          In the remaining class of jet VTOL propulsion concepts, the engine
      airflow is split, and the fan air is ducted away from the core air (Fig. 21 .7).

The core air is exited through a vectoring nozzle and is deflected downward
for vertical flight.
     In forward flight the fan air goes out an aft-facing nozzle, whereas in ver­
ti cal flight the fan air is ducted forward for balance. The fan air is usually aug­
mented in some fashion to increase total thrust in vertical flight. The remote
augmented lift system (RALS) acts like an afterburner. Fuel is added to the
fan air and burned before exiting through a front nozzle. Gas-driven fans
and ejectors can also be used to augment the fan-air thrust. These act in
the manner already described.
     In addition to the concepts just described, there are many possible com­
binations of these basic VTOL propulsion schemes. An advanced Harrier­
like supersonic fighter was proposed to incorporate a PCB Pegasus-type
engine as well as separate lift engines. The astounding Dornier Do 31,
designed to carry 36 soldiers into combat, flew in 1967 with two Pegasus
engines and eight Rolls Royce lift engines. The noise when hovering must
have been unbelievable. This, the only vertical takeoff jet transport ever
built, is also unusual in that it never crashed during its flight-test program
and is honorably retired to a museum near Munich.

#lfJJ Vectoring Nozzle Types
    The selection of the type of nozzle-vectoring mechanism is almost as
important to a VTOL aircraft design as the type of propulsion system. The
ideal vectoring mechanism would weigh little more than a conventional
nozzle and would provide continuous vectoring from 0 to over 90 deg with
negligible thrust loss. Such a nozzle has yet to be designed.
    The common types of VTOL nozzle are shown in Fig. 21.8. The most
obvious means of vectoring the thrust, vectoring flaps (Fig. 21 .8a), deflect
the engine flow much as wi_ng flaps deflect the external airflow. These vector­
ing flaps can be an integral part of the nozzle system, as shown. This type of
vectoring system introduces a thrust loss of roughly 3-6% when vectored
90 deg.
    The vectoring flaps can also be external to the nozzle as a part of the wing
flap system. This approach was used on the XC- 1 5 transport prototype.
Although this was not a VTOL aircraft, its wing flap system was able to
turn the engine flow more than 60 deg for STOL landings. This, combined
with a landing gear that permits a 30-deg nose-up position, would provide
the required 90 deg of total thrust vectoring for vertical flight.
    The bucket vectoring mechanism (Fig. 2 1 .8b) is similar to the commonly
used clamshell thrust reverser. The great advantage of this concept is that
the flow turning forces are all carried through the hinge line; thus, the actua­
tor can be fairly small. Also, the bucket can be designed with a smooth
turning surface to raise the turning efficiency. A bucket vectoring nozzle
can be designed to have a thrust loss of only about 2-3% when vectored
90 deg.
