     Asymmetric Airplanes
       Most aircraft design is done assuming a plane of symmetry-we usually
  de sign  just the left half of the aircraft and assume that the other side is a
  mirror image. This simplifies design, but even more important, it simplifies
  late ral-directional stability and handling qualities. Specifically, with a
  sym metric design we can usually assume that the rolling and yawing
  moments are zero when the aircraft is at zero sideslip angle regardless of
  angle of attack, and that these moments increment the same whether a
  right or left sideslip occurs.
       This is generally true for gliders and jets, although the asymmetric for­
  mation of vortices on the nose is always a potential problem (Chapter 8).
  For propeller-powered aircraft, this assumption is often untrue or irrelevant.
      A tractor-propeller aircraft is flying in its own propwash, and that prop­
 wash includes a rotational motion. Thus, the aircraft can have a symmetric
 flowfield only if it has multiple propellers that rotate in opposite directions
 on opposite sides of the aircraft. Otherwise, a physically symmetric
 prop-powered aircraft flies in a nonsymmetric flowfield, so that it acts like a
 nonsymmetric aircraft. Furthermore, the p-effect described in Chapter 16
 includes the fact that the center of thrust of a propeller moves laterally
 when the disk of the propeller is at an angle of attack to the flow, as during a
 climb. This causes a yawing moment, even for a symmetric aircraft.
      Most designers, faced with these problems, design a physically symmetric
 aircraft that will fly symmetrically when power is turned off and then try to fix
 these power-induced effects with trim and by using tricks such as angling the
 vertical tail or the engine thrust axis. Other designers have reasoned, "since it
 isn't going to fly symmetrically anyway, why does it have to look symmetric?"
 They have even thought of ways to use nonsymmetric geometry to make it fly
 more symmetrically!
      An early example was the German Blohm-Voss Bv- 141, flown in 1938
 (Fig. 23.9). By placing the pilot and tail gunner in a pod offset from the
main fuselage containing the engine and tails, the gunner was afforded a
clear field of fire while the pilot got unsurpassed downward visibility for a
single-engine attack aircraft. The p-effect moved the thrust axis to the
right, closer to the centerline, and made the flying characteristics far more
symmetrical than the aircraft's appearance would indicate.
      Figure 23. 10 shows Burt Rutan's Boomerang. While the designer of the
Bv- 141 kept a symmetrical wing and carefully balanced the aircraft masses
on each side of its center, the Boomerang is so wildly nonsymmetric that
one suspects Rutan was just showing off, until you follow through his logic
and realize that everything on the design has a reason.
     First, Boomerang had to be twin-engine for safety, but the actual statistics
in dicate that a twin is no safer than a single-engine aircraft. Although having
an extra engine can save you if you lose an engine over the Alps at midnight,
you also get a doubled risk of having one engine fail. In a conventional design
848     A i r c raft Des i g n : A Conceptual Approach




                   F i g . 23.9   Single-engine asymmetric design: Blohm-Voss Bv-1 4 1 .


        the loss of an engine on takeoff or go-around requires expert piloting to
       avoid a crash. In fact, most twins have a minimum engine-out flying speed
       that is higher than the stall speed, and if the pilot allows the aircraft to fall
       below that speed the running engine will drag the aircraft over on its back
       or into a spin.
           The p-effect makes this worse. If the running engine has its downward­
       traveling blade away from the fuselage (right-hand engine for most aircraft),
       the p-effect moves the thrust axis even farther out, increasing the
      yawing moments.
           The way to minimize the engine-out yawing is to get the two propellers as
      close to each other and the centerline of the aircraft as is possible. A normal,
      fuselage-plus-two-nacelle layout has a minimum propeller separation equal
      to the width of the fuselage plus a reasonable allowance for propeller
      clearance. This is too much to avoid a yawing problem. Instead, Boomerang
      is designed starting with a single fuselage with an engine in front, as if it were
                                C H A PT E R 23   Desi g n of U n i q u e A i rcraft Concepts   849


to be a single-engine aircraft. A second engine is added alongside, not in a
"copycat" fuselage as with the F-82, but in a much smaller engine nacelle.
Of course, this makes the design nonsymmetrical, but who cares?! The pro­
peller tips are laterally separated by only 1 ft {30 cm}, and the aircraft lateral
center of gravity winds up somewhere between the two bodies. With the
engines so close together, the plane flies with almost no rudder input no
matter which engine fai!s. l165l
    To reduce propeller mutual interference and to better balance the design,
the extra engine is moved to the rear as far as possible without having the
plane of the propeller disk intersect the passenger compartment. This
reduces noise and avoids the risk of a thrown blade cutting someone in
half. This also moves the extra nacelle far enough back that, with a slight
stretch, it can be attached to the horizontal tail to increase torsional rigidity
and save some structural weight-the same trick used on the Voyager. Wings
are swept forward to allow positioning the wing root as far away from the left
propeller as possible, to avoid interference.




   Fig. 23. 1 0   Twin-engine asymmetric design: Rutan Boomerang original design layout
                                  (courtesy of E. Rutan).
850     A i rc raft Des i g n : A C o n c e p tu a l A p p r o a c h




                                     Fig. 23. 1 1    Asymmetric "safety" twin.


           Rutan says the following:

             P-effect makes this aircraft (fly) symmetrical at low speeds, as the thrust lines
             move right. The combination of having half of the lateral arm for engine-out
             and about twice the directional stability of conventional twins (long tail arms
             and both tails in prop wash) gives a very dramatic benefit-this aircraft can be
             flown at full aft stick and you can feather one engine and apply full power to
             the other under complete control while not touching the rudder pedals! In
             this condition it takes l lb (1.5 deg) of aileron to hold heading. You can
             also do aggressive turning maneuvering at full aft stick using only the
             stick. l166l

       The asymmetry of the Boomerang extends to the cabin. The seats are stag­
       gered front to rear rather than being lined up, shoulder to shoulder. This
       allows a narrower fuselage, and thus reduced frontal area yet provides
       plenty of shoulder room for all.
           Figure 23. 1 1 shows another take on the layout of an asymmetric "safety"
      twin, developed as a design example for this author's book Simplified Aircraft
      Design for HomebuildersJ1l This approach brings the engines closer together
      by starting with a normal single-engine GA design layout but adding a second
      engine as a wing-mounted pusher. Because a propeller's thrust line moves
      towards the downward-moving blade when the airplane is at an angle of
      attack, this arrangement puts the thrust axis of both propellers even closer
      to the aircraft lateral center during the critical climb-out phase.

rf1 Joined Wi ng
     A number of aircraft have had biplane wings "joined" in some fashion, at
 or near the tips. Often such joining was in the form of vertical endplate or
 similar panel and had little or no structural implications. Julian Wolkovitch
proposed a different and more sophisticated concept in which triangulation is
used to enhance structural strength. l167l The "joined wing" has two wings, a
 front wing that is swept to the rear and a back wing that is swept toward the
front. The back wing is mounted at the top of the vertical tail and extends
downward at a substantial anhedral angle (negative dihedral), meeting and
attaching to the front wing. From the front this has a triangular shape,
whereas from the top, a diamond shape.
     Figure 23. 12 illustrates two notional joined wing concepts. The lower
version, where the wings join somewhere in the middle of the front wing's
span, seems preferable according to most studies.
     The main benefit is the substantial reduction in wing structural weight
that is achievable, on the order of 30%. This results from the triangulation,
                                         '
with the back wing acting as strut for the front wing. Also, the actual net
force vector of a wing is upward (lift) and to the rear (drag), so this arrange­
ment is actually more triangulated than it appears: the net force vector is
aligned with the plane of the two wings better than if the front wing were
above the back wing as in some other joined concepts.
    With the loads in the plane of triangulation carried by that triangulation,
only the out-of-plane loads are carried by normal wing bending structure.
Here an additional structural benefit is obtained-the out-of-plane loads
are partly carried by the vertical distance between the wing panels' front
and rear spars, measured in the direction perpendicular to the plane of




                        Fig. 23. 1 2   Joined-wing concepts.
852   A i rc raft Des i g n : A C o n c e ptu a l A p p r o a c h




                                                                                     __   \


                                                                                Effective
                                                                               box depth



                                 Fig. 23. 1 3    Joined-wing structural benefits.

      triangulation. This increases the effective wing-box depth for structural
      purposes (Fig. 23. 13).
          On the negative side, it is difficult to get a trimmed maximum lift coeffi­
      cient equal to a normal wing-tail configuration because you cannot balance
      out large flaps on the back wing. This would cause excess wetted area, and
      there might be extra interference drag with so many tight component
      intersections.
          The joined-wing configuration has been proposed by Boeing as a carrier­
      based surveillance aircraft, with antennas on all four wing panels to provide
      coverage in all directions. This author did an unpublished design study at
      Rockwell where the joined wing was used for VTOL because without a big
      wing root at the center of gravity, the suckdown effect might be reduced.

             Some More Innovative Wings
          Aircraft innovators seek improvements in all parts of the aircraft but
      seem to focus especially upon the wing. Their "great ideas" include better air­
      foils, new wing-tip shapes, exotic winglets, and exciting, wild wing arrange­
      ments. Perhaps this makes sense: the wing is what sets the airplane apart
      from other vehicles, and the wing generates all of the lift and causes much
      of the drag and weight. Of course, it should draw the attention of innovators,
      but sometimes it seems that they have gone a little too far!
          A number of innovative wing arrangements have already been mentioned
      including flying wings, delta wings, joined wings, and forward-swept wings.
      Here are a few more.

      #!QI Tandem Wing
          The tandem wing was discussed in Chapter 4 where its promise and
      fundamental problems were outlined. The promise is a theoretical 50%
      savings in induced drag, but this only applies if the span is kept the same
      as the equivalent single wing being replaced. In other words, each wing
                              C HAPTE R 23    Desi g n of U n i q u e Ai rcraft Concepts   853

 panel must have twice the aspect ratio of the equivalent area single wing.
 Tandem-wing designs are rarely drawn this way, and Fig. 23.14 shows why:
 this design's long, skinny wings would be far heavier and offer little volume
 for fuel and landing gear, but if "normal" looking wings are drawn, the
 induced drag is actually increased because the total span is reduced.
      This design, like other tandem-wing designs, cannot have large flaps on
 the back wing because it would be impossible to trim out their moments.
 This requires a greater total wing area to make up for the poor maximum
 lift coefficient, adding to the wetted area and weight. f12l
      The tandem wing does have its uses. A large payload can be efficiently
 carried between the two wings. This author used the tandem-wing arrange­
 ment to carry a massive air-launched ICBM in a never-built design done for
Rockwell. f2l The Scaled Composites White Knight suspends SpaceShipOne
between its tandem wings. Scaled's record-holding Proteus, named after an
appearance-changing Greek god, has a removable fuselage section between
its two wings so that different payload geometries can be installed without
grounding the whole airplane.
      The design of a tandem-wing aircraft has unique challenges. Location of
the main landing gear is especially problematic because neither wing is near
the center of gravity. Wing internal volume is reduced by the square-cube law
described in Chapter 19: a half-size wing only has 35% of the volume, so two
of them have only 70% of the original volume. This affects fuel tanks and
landing gear.
      To minimize the aerodynamic penalties of a tandem-wing design, it is
desirable to separate the two wings as far apart as possible, both horizontally
and vertically. It is best if the front wing is low and the back wing is high, to
maximize the vertical separation of the downwash from the back wing.
      However, watch out that the disturbed air shed when the front wing stalls
does not go over the rear wing and make it stall too. The opposite effect is
also possible. The original Flying Flea had so many crashes that it was




                    Fig. 23. 1 4   Tandem-wing subsonic transport.
854   A i r c raft Desi g n : A C o n c e pt u a l A p p r o a c h


      banned in some countries, until it was discovered that under some situation s
      the airflow off the front wing would blow over the top of the back win g,
      increasing its lift and forcing the nose into the ground.

      #.flfJ Box Wing
          The wild-looking box wing was studied at Lockheed in the 1960s. It is
      basically a tandem wing with vertical endplates attaching the tips (see
      Fig. 23. 15). It promises less induced drag for the same span and supposedly
      has a good transonic area distribution that increases the critical
      Mach number. There probably isn't a significant structural savings because
      unlike Wolkovitch's Joined Wing, the geometry doesn't provide any
      triangularization.
          Drawbacks include the weight of the wings, the wetted area and weight of
      the endplates, problems packaging the landing gear, and an inability to put
      big flaps on the back wing. Studies have found weird flutter modes whose
      prevention would probably add even more weight. But, there are still
      people who love the box wing, and maybe they are right for some application.


      #.flfJ C-Wing
          The C-wing is an extension of the winglet concept, being literally a
      winglet on a winglet (see Fig. 23. 16). This provides the same drag reduction
      for the winglet that the winglet provides to the wing. The final surface is
      horizontal, and if all three surfaces are swept, it is far enough to the rear to
      serve as the horizontal tail. To work properly, that last surface has a download
      so that the C-wing potentially' gets its stabilizing trim force for free.




                                            Fig. 23. 1 5    Box wing .
                                    CHAPTER 23       Des i g n o f U n i q u e Ai rc raft Concepts   855




                      (�-)------
                       ,.--·- . .      , • "•"'.,




    _c ______




                                      Fig. 23. 1 6    C-wing.


    The obvious problem, though, is the structure. These tip-mounted
surfaces would cause substantial twisting in the wing, especially if used as
control surfaces. There will be a large weight penalty and a potential
for flutter.
    The C-wing isn't as crazy as it looks. Boeing and Stanford University have
studied C-Wing concepts, including the application of the C-wing to the
blended wing body already discussed. Wind-tunnel tests are promising. For
an overview of C-Wing and other nonplanar wing concepts, see lecture
notes by Stanford profess o r Ilan Kroo. l168l
    This notional C-wing design was for a B-737-class commercial transport
but wasn't analyzed in detaiI. [12]


#fUI Oblique Wing
    Another variant of the asymmetric design offers the theoretical minimum
drag, maximum efficiency supersonic design. The oblique wing is a swept
wing with one side swept forward and the other swept to the rear, that is,
a single straight wing skewed with respect to the fuselage. This is usually
pivoted at the center to allow variable sweep, which for this concept is easy
to mechanize with little weight penalty.
    Because the wing structural box is straight, the oblique wing is much
lighter in weight than other swept wings. It obtains the same transonic and
supersonic benefits as other swept wings and is no worse than the aft-swept
856   A i r c raft D e s i g n : A C o n c e p tu a l A p p roa c h


      wing as to stall angle. Because the aft-swept wing will likely stall first, a stall
      limiter of some sort is desirable.
          The main advantage, though, is the supersonic wave drag. Because the left
      wing and right wing are not at the same fuselage station (distance from the
      nose), they do not add to each other in the aircraft's volume distribution.
      The wing's volume is "spread" in the flight direction, reducing the aircraft's
      maximum cross-section area-and wave drag varies by the square of the
      maximum cross-section area [Eq. (12.45)] .
          The oblique wing seems most suitable fo r a supersonic transport. It was
      under serious consideration for a Navy attack fighter, but it is problematic if
      stealth is desired.
          In a recent study for NASA, this author looked at the oblique wing for a
      subsonic transport. Benefits include a higher critical Mach number, a
      reduced wing weight (the wing box is structurally unswept), and with wing
      unswept and large flaps deployed, an increased maximum lift allowing the
      wing to be smaller. The problems include the extra weight of the pivot and
      mechanisms, and difficulties in packaging the landing gear. This concept,
      shown in Fig. 23. 17, places the wing on a short pedestal to minimize interfer­
      ence effects and to prevent the wing wake from entering the inlet duct.

      #&j Active Aeroelastic Wing
          There is one advanced aircraft technology that offers 10% wing weight
      savings, gust alleviation, drag modulation, and improved three-axis flight




                                Fig. 23. 1 7     Oblique-wing subsonic transport.
                                   C HAPTE R 23     Desi g n of U n i q u e Aircraft Concepts         857

 control. Properly applied, it could allow a wing of higher aspect ratio with
 little or no weight penalty. It has been studied for years and proven in super­
 sonic flight test. It is applicable to fighters, transports, and most other classes
 of aircraft. But for some strange reason, this technology has become lost to
 the sands of time.
      The active aeroelastic wing (AAW) was developed at Rockwell Inter­
 national* to solve problems with excessive flexibility in Rockwell's Advanced
 Tactical Fighter design (Fig. 7.2). AAW was first conceived as a computerized
 implementation of a portion of every B-47 pilot's training. The B-47, with its
 swept high-aspect-ratio wings, had such bad aileron roll reversal (see Chapter
 16) that flight was normally restricted to below 455 kt {840 km/h} . Above
 that speed, B-47 pilots practiced flying the airplane "backwards," moving
 the stick to the right to roll the bomber to the left. AAW does this, and
 much more.
      In the active aeroelastic wing the wing box is deliberately designed with
 reduced torsional stiffness, while of normal strength in all other directions.
This saves weight because torsional stiffness requirements are often the
most critical loads on the outer third of the wing. High-speed actuators are
used on leading- and trailing-edge control surfaces. These are capable of
deflecting up as well as down. The whole thing is controlled with a compu­
terized control system, which deflects those surfaces as required.
      For roll control, the trailing-edge surfaces deflect like normal ailerons at
low speeds, creating lift on that side of the wing (Fig. 23. 18a). The illustration
shows the AAW surfaces on the left wing of a notional advanced transport, so
this would roll the airplane to the right. At higher speeds the ailerons twist
the wing so much that the net force is downwards (Fig. 23. 1 8b), rolling the
airplane to the left. Downward deflection of the leading-edge flaps produces
a download at the front of the wing box, twisting the wing leading edge down
even more (Fig. 23.18c) . .
     AAW even allows the creation of additional wing-tip drag for yaw control
and to act as speed brakes. This is done by deflecting the leading- and
trailing-edge surfaces so that they "fight" each other, each trying to twist
the wing in the opposite direction. As shown (Fig. 23. 1 8e), this would yaw
the airplane to the left.
     AAW is often compared to the wing warping in the Wright Flyer, but
that was accomplished mechanically, with control wires pulled by the pilot.
Another comparison is to the servotab flight control systems used by
airplanes as large and fast as the Boeing 707, where the ailerons had no
mechanical actuation. Instead, the control system moved a small tab
surface at the back of the aileron. This moved the aileron, and the aileron
rolled the airplane. AAW is wing warping, mechanized with servotabs.

    * The original name of the AAW was "active flexible adaptive wing," but people pronounced it
"awful" so a new name was invented. Despite the awful name, the wing remains very strong. Ed Pen­
dleton, USAF program manager for X-53, said, "! can still walk all the way out on the wing tip, and
stand there and jump up and down on it."

                                           Fig. 23. 1 8        Active aeroelastic wing.

           While normally used for roll, this wing-twisting ability can also be used to
       twist both wings leading edge down, reducing lift out at the tips. This can be
       used for gust alleviation, quickly reducing the lift when a gust is encountered .
       It can also be used for optimizing spanwise lift distribution at different flight
       conditions, minimizing induced drag.
           If the wing is swept enough, simultaneous twisting of both wing tips can
       provide pitch control much like the elevons of a flying wing. With this, the
       AAW can provide roll, pitch, yaw, and drag control, all at once!
           In-depth aircraft design studies showed that when the wing weight
       savings is applied to allow a higher-aspect-ratio wing, there is a total sized
       takeoff gross weight reduction of nearly 20% for a supersonic design like a
      fighter and 10% for a transonic design like a commercial transport.
           This all sounds far-fetched, but the active aeroelastic wing was already
      flight tested as a joint project of the Air Force Research Laboratory,
      Boeing, and NASA Dryden. An F-18, renamed X-53, was modified to make
      its wings more flexible. It made over 50 flights, half of which were supersonic.
      AAW works, no question. However, its application to transports and other
      high-aspect-ratio designs has still not been flight tested.
          Active aeroelastic wing technology was assumed for the advanced trans­
      port design of Fig. 4.36 and was used for roll, pitch, and yaw control at high
      speeds. This tailless design, also shown in Fig. 23.18, saved 10% in wetted area
      and attains a 60% reduction in fuel consumption. AAW would be equally
      beneficial for more normal configurations and, in one form or another, will
      probably be common in the future. Perhaps it won't even be called AAW
      and will just be another mode of a complicated flight control system.

     Wi ng-in-Ground-Effect
     Equation (12.60) is tantalizing. If we could fly very close to the ground,
say, at a height of 1/20 of the wing span, we would have an induced drag
that is only 27% of normal. Furthermore, the lift coefficient increases near
the ground allowing us to fly with a smaller wing-if we can stay at such
low heights.
     It would be difficult to imagine flying from Los Angeles to Chicago at a
height of 5 ft { 1 .5 m}, but Los Angeles to Tokyo might be feasible! An aircraft
designed like a flying boat but intended to keep within ground effect offers
fantastic L/ D. Called "wing-in-ground-effect" (WIG), such designs were
built and flown by Lippisch and others, most notably the Russians. They
call such aircraft "Ekrano-planes" and have built huge ones, both propeller
and jet powered.
     During the Cold War, satellite photos detected something immense flying
very fast over the Caspian Sea, which was soon nicknamed the "Caspian Sea
Monster." It turned out to be the Bartini-Beriev VVA-14 or KM (Russian
abbreviation for prototype ship). Depicted in Fig. 23.19, it was designed by
the Central Hydrofoil Design Bureau and first flown in 1966. Weighing 1 . 1
million l b {500,000 kg}, i t has eight turbojets mounted o n a stub pylon at
the front of the fuselage. Their exhausts can be deflected down to the
water in front of the wing to create an air cushion for added lift (a technique
called power-augmented ram or PAR). The KM has two more turbojets
mounted on the vertical tail for extra thrust during takeoff and was said to
cruise at 230 kt {430 km/h}. Unfortunately, the only KM ever built crashed
during takeoff in 1980.
    More recently, there was a substantial program at Boeing for a giant tur­
boprop WIG military transport. Called Pelican, it was not a seaplane, taking
off from runways then descending to fly at less than 50 ft { 1 5 m} height when
over water. It would also be capable of flying as a normal airplane but with far
less range when out-of-ground effect. A true monster, it would be about
400 ft {122 m} long with an even greater wingspan and would supposedly




                  Fig. 23. 1 9   Russian "Caspian Sea Monster" WIG.
860    Aircraft Desig n : A Conceptu a l Approach

        have a useful load of 2.8 m lb {1.3 m kg}. However, Pelican seems to have
       been a study more than a serious development program and has not b ee n
       heard from in almost a decade.
           The WIG concept works best for a very large vehicle because the height
       required to miss the waves is a smaller percentage of the wing span for a large
       vehicle. Also, the WIG is almost by definition a flying boat and needs a sea­
       plane hull as described in Sec. 1 1 .7. This will cause a substantial weight and
       drag penalty. If a relatively small wing is used to minimize drag, then getting
       out of the water becomes a real problem. Use of PAR and extra engines as just
       described can help, but results in additional weight and complexity penalties.
       Finally, operation considerations must be addressed early in the design.
       Where will it dock? How will passengers and payload be loaded? How will
       maintenance be done? What new infrastructure will be required? These
       must all be determined before a design can be finalized and assessed as to
       economic feasibility.

             Unmanned/U n i n ha bited Aircraft
            Unmanned aircraft have been a part of aviation since before the Wright
        Brothers. Several made credible flights before 1 903, although without the
       means of control that separated the Wright Brothers from other early
       aviation pioneers. Today, the vast computational capabilities that can be
       put into a tiny chip are bringing about a renaissance in the field of unmanned
       aircraft.
           The names that we apply to an airplane "with nobody inside" are many,
       and the preferred term keeps changing. "Drone" (as in "target") and "RPV"
       (remotely piloted vehicle) were the normal names from the 1930s until
       well into the 1980s. Those phrases have become obsolete largely because
       the newer unmanned aircraft are not "flown" in real time by a remote oper­
       ator who manipulates a control stick like an onboard pilot. Instead, an
       onboard computerized flight control system uses GPS and satellite links to
      fly itself, with the on-the-ground human only giving mission directions.
           Today the most common terminology is UAV, for Unmanned Air
      Vehicle. In some circles "uninhabited" is preferred to "unmanned," appar­
      ently for nontechnical reasons. "Aerial" is sometimes preferred rather than
      "air." The FAA now prefers simply "UA" for unmanned aircraft. If commer­
      cial airliners are ever flow entirely by computer, the term "unpiloted" could
      be applied. Recently, the word "drone" has been resurrected and applied to
      small quadcopters. Pay attention, the terminology will change again!
          There are many UAVs of various types in operation around the world.
      Many are target drones, such as the Mach 4 AQM-37. A number are for
      surveillance or are multipurpose, such as the Israel Aircraft Industry
      Hunter. Most UAV designs range in size and technology from the equivalent
      of large model airplanes (Fig. 23.20) to an uninhabited general aviation
      aircraft, although a few UAVs are larger and highly sophisticated.
                               C HA PT E R 23   Desi g n of U n i q u e Ai rcraft Concepts      86 1




Fig. 23.20   Boeing Educationa l Project UAV (D. Raymer and R. Dellacamera, Instructor/Design
                                     Consultants, 2005) .


     The General Atomics Predator is typical of prop-powered, low-speed
UAVs, It is used for surveillance in trouble spots around the world. Predator
is a pusher-propeller aircraft constructed much like a composite homebuilt
aircraft. Weighing about 1900 lb {862 kg}, it flies at about l lO kt {204 km/
h} and can operate for a total of over 40 hours. Under continuous operator
control, Predator carries visual light and infrared television cameras and
                           _
can also carry a ground-looking radar.
     The larger, jet-powered Global Hawk is built by Northrop-Grumman
(Ryan) and is somewhat similar in design and mission to an unmanned
U-2. Cruising at 65,000 ft {19,812 m} with a total range of 16,566 n
miles {30,680 km}, Global Hawk has a takeoff gross weight of 25,600 lb
{1 1,612 kg}, It carries a payload of electronic sensors including electro­
optical, infrared, and synthetic aperture radar with moving target
indicator.
     Kratos Unmanned Systems, formerly Composite Engineering Inc., has
gone from a composite fabrication house to a major producer of transonic
and supersonic jet UAVs, They've delivered hundreds of BQM- 167 transonic
target drones and begun production of the BQM-177 A, supersonic without
afterburning due to its sleek design and aggressive area ruling. Nicknamed
"Dos Equis" during early flight tests, the BQM- 177 exceeds 40,000 ft and
can sustain 6-g turns. It also goes M0.95 at sea level and is programmed to
simulate the trajectories of sea-skimming antiship missiles. Figure 23.21
862      A i r c raft De s i g n : A C o n c e p tu a l A p p ro a c h


         shows the flight test version; the production version have a W-shaped win g
         trailing edge and a few other minor changes.*
             Design of a VAV is much like the design of any other aircraft but with
        special considerations for takeoff and landing and for provision of avi o nics
        and systems for uninhabited flight. Options for takeoff are many, incl udi n g
        conventional wheeled takeoff and landing, use of a launching rail, air or
        car launch, boosted vertical launch, and others. For landing, op tion s
        include wheels, skids, parachutes, airbags, and none-that is, keep it flying
        forever or j ust let it crash! Trade studies should be done to compare
        these alternatives.
            The removal of the aircrew from the design requirements does not save as
        much in weight or cost as some might assume. The requirements for cooling
       air are often based on avionics, not crew members, and a VAV probably will
       require more avionics to do a given mission. While it is tempting to assume
       that we can remove redundancy, reliability, and structural strength margins
       from an aircraft that has no crew members, we must consider the safety of
       people on the ground. A VAV that is not permitted to operate over land
       has little operational utility.
            A detailed weights and sizing analysis should reveal a reduction in sized
       takeoff gross weight of perhaps 10 - 30% compared to an "inhabited" aircraft.
       The design layout should benefit from the absence of a cockpit and canopy.
       Depending on the takeoff and landing gear chosen, further savings in volume

by reducing the required ultimate load factor, assuming that it will not fly in

     In the weights equations of Chapter 15, the use of 0. 5 - 0. 7 for the number
of crew members will approximate the systems that remain even when an air­
craft has no crew members aboard.
    With modern computer and guidance capabilities, it has become feasible
to use unmanned systems for a variety of tactical applications including drop­
ping bombs and even air-to-air dogfighting. Advanced tactical unmanned
aircraft can attack known-location targets using a variety of conventional
payloads such as "smart" bombs, programmed to hit a particular GPS coor­
dinate. With a more aggressive application of technology, even relocatable
targets and targets of opportunity could be attacked by a VAV, and such air­
craft are in development around the world. An air-to-air combat VAV is also
conceivable and could have a g-limit double the human tolerance or more.
    Figure 23.22 shows a notional design concept for a tactical unmanned/
uninhabited air vehicle done at Conceptual Research Corporation for inves­
tigation of alternative and novel concepts for inlets and exhaust nozzles for
such aircraft. While this concept was conceived to simply drop a smart
bomb on a predetermined GPS coordinate location, it could also carry sur­
veillance, reconnaissance, and communications relay equipment for
alternative missions.


'fl Derivative Aircraft Design
    The design of a derivative of an existing airplane is probably the least
innovative thing we designers are called upon to do, but sometimes it takes
the most innovative thinking. The problem is simple: whatever we are
trying to do with the modified airplane is constrained by the reality of the
existing airplane. For a blank-sheet-of-paper design, if we need a little
more wing span, we can redraw a few lines or type a few commands into
864     A i rc raft Des i g n : A Conceptu a l Approach

          the CAD program. For a derivative design, we need to know if it is feasible
          and affordable to extend the wing span.
              Will the wing center section take the extra load? If not, it needs to be
          strengthened, which will increase the cost. Does the extended wing tip
          strike the ground in a bad landing? If so, the landing gear legs might need
         lengthening which is nearly impossible for most airplanes. If the aircraft
         total weight increases, can the landing gear handle the loads and are the
         tires big enough? Is the rudder big enough to handle the extra yawing
         moments? It goes on and on, and if some real-world constraint is ignored
         or forgotten, the project fails.
              In fact, you really cannot complete the conceptual design of an aircraft
         derivative until you've taken an in-depth look at some aspects that would
         normally be considered a detail design issue, like the stress calculations of
         the wing center section. There is a cost step function: it is fairly cheap to
         extend the wing span until you reach the length where the extra load requires
         a wing center-section redesign, and then the cost suddenly goes up a lot. You
         need to know where that is before you can decide how much to extend the
        wing span. There are no top-level, rule-of-thumb estimations. You need to
        do the real calculations.
             Luckily, most airplanes have some growth allowances built in. The
        landing gear of new aircraft are usually designed with a 25% increase in
        gross weight, to allow for future growth. There is sometimes extra volume
        in less accessible parts of the aircraft such as near the wing tips, which can
       be converted to fuel tanks if need be. A design might have extra ground clear­
        ance to allow for later retrofitting with a bigger propeller or larger turbofan.
             In some cases, a new design will deliberately have an entire series of pre­
       planned product improvements (P 3 I) built in, with a clever configuration that
       allows a later fuselage stretch, or winglet addition, or re-engining, etc. A
       similar process is called "spiral development," a term from the software
       industry and implying a bit less preplanning but a continuous improvement
       process nonetheless. We pilots shudder at any use of the word "spiral" in con­
       nection with an aircraft-the phrase "death spiral" comes to mind!
            Certain aspects of an aircraft create extreme problems for derivative air­
       craft. It is very difficult to increase the allowable total aircraft weight for a
       given landing-gear system, once the built-in growth allowance is used up.
       The shock-struts need greater diameter. The strut itself needs to be stronger,
      and the strut forgings are both expensive and long-lead fabrication items.
      The tires cannot have their pressure raised to carry the greater load; that
      will damage the runways. If the tires are made larger, they won't fit inside
      the wheel wells. The brakes inside the tires need greater physical size and
      mass to stop the heavier airplane.
            Ground clearance can restrict propeller size or podded engine diameter.
      For an internal jet engine, it is almost impossible to increase the diameter of
      the internal inlet duct. An entire redesign is necessary, as was done for the
      F-86H and the British Nimrod.
                           C HAPTE R 23   Desi g n of U n i q u e Ai rcraft Concepts   865

    There is the whole issue of "interoperability" with the current fleet. You
probably want to use the same materials and fabrication processes, both for
production and later maintenance. You would like for the pilots of the
current airplane to be able to fly the derivative with minimal training and
hopefully avoid the need for a new "type rating" for the pilots. This requires
minimal changes to the cockpit controls and instruments, flying qualities,
and emergency procedures. Again, these are all issues that are normally con­
sidered in detail design but must be resolved before the derivative aircraft
con figuration can be finalized.
    Typical changes for a derivative aircraft include:
• Increased takeoff gross weight
• Increased avionics
• Increased payload weight

• Additional payload types

• External fuel and/ or payload

• Increased fuel

• Increased thrust from current engine .

• Re-engine (i.e., new engine type)

• Wing tip or root extension

• Winglets

• New wing

• Fuselage stretch (watch the tail-down ground angle)

• Scab-on pods and pallets



    For those of us in conceptual design, there is a problem when we work on
a derivative design study. Our analysis tools, suitable for conceptual design,
are forced to almost perfectly match the known capabilities of the original
airplane. Otherwise, nobody will believe the numbers for the modified air­
plane. This often requires "tweaking" and "fudge-factoring" the analysis
inputs until the correct answers are obtained.
    Once we have calibrated the analysis to the unmodified aircraft and can
match the range and key performance points, we can define the required
changes to the geometry and estimate the revised aerodynamics including
the effects of increased wetted area, revised wing planform, and possibly
component interferences.
    We must also estimate the impact of the design changes on the empty
weight. This can be difficult, and our usual statistical equations might not
give us the right answer. The weight of a modified part is greater than the
weight of that part if designed all new. Often, a simple pounds-per-square­
foot method is better than a sophisticated statistical equation. The best
answer, though, is a detail weights buildup of the additional parts.
    If there is a change to propulsion, the new values for thrust and SFC must
be estimated. Next, we calculate range and performance for the modified air­
craft using the above methods. Hopefully, it all seems reasonable; if not, find
out why!
866   A i rc raft D e s i g n : A Conceptu a l A p proach


           The estimation of the cost of a derivative aircraft program is very diffic ult.
       You cannot estimate cost by analyzing the revised design as if it were new an d
       then analyzing the cost of the original design using the same methods, then
       subtracting one from the other. This does not work! Not even the proven
       methods of Chapter 1 8 can be applied in this fashion.
           The best cost estimation is through a detailed work-breakdown-structure
       (WBS) buildup, detailing the actual tasks required to fly and produce the air­
      craft. This should be done using actual data for the aircraft being modified,
      but this is difficult to obtain.
           A simple cost-estimation method for derivative aircraft design comes from
      the RAND Corporation, source of the DAPCA method of Chapter 18. A stat­
      istical analysis of various derivative projects was performed yielding straight
      lines on log-log graph paper. These can be used to estimate the labor hours
      for the new parts of a derivative aircraft (see (169] ). While based only upon
      1 1 military fighters, bombers, and transports, it seems reasonable for most
      classes of aircraft until better data are available. Take no credit for the old
      parts which are "thrown away." Nobody reimburses you for those "returns."




                                  What We've Learned

       Innovative aircraft concepts are a l o t of fu n and are sometimes worthwhile,
       but designers need to study them with a "show-me" mentality focusing on
       weight, wetted area, and trimmed maximum lift.

        Introd uction


T
          his final chapter offers two design examples that illustrate the con­
          cepts and methods presented in this book. These are a single-seat aero­
          batic homebuilt airplane, and a lightweight supercruise dogfighter.
     These examples illustrate the steps and thought processes used in
 conceptual design covering the extremes from propeller-powered, fixed-size
engine design to "rubber.- engine" supersonic design. The differences and
similarities between these extremes of design are shown.
     Design requirements for these aircraft were assumed based upon data for
similar aircraft. These design requirements were then treated as if they were
mandated by some customer and used as the starting point for the design effort.
     The examples are designed and analyzed using the methods presented
in the book. Every effort has been made by the author to develop credible,
realistic designs and to analyze and optimize them properly. However, no
claim is made that these are optimal designs or even good designs or that
all calculations are correct!
     Furthermore, the examples are incomplete in that only the more impor­
tant analysis areas are presented due to space limitations. Were the author to
grade himself in a college design course, these examples would rate at most a
"B." The "A" students would conduct far more analysis (structures, roll rate,
e.g. envelopes, etc.) and would ultimately redraw the as-optimized aircraft to
ensure that the analysis assumptions were realistic.


                                                                                                       867
  868    A i rcraft De s i g n : A Conceptu a l A p p roach


              The first example is designed and analyzed completely by hand with
         pocket calculator to show that this initial design process is fully understand­
         able. The author even fought to show the original hand-written analysis work
         rather than having it typed. Students can go through it and say, " . . . anybo dy
         can do that!"
             The only exception to the by-hand rule is that a simple computer
         program was used for stepping through the sizing iterations. It could have
         been done by hand using the methods of Chapter 3, but life is too short.
         This simple program is available (free) at the author's website, www.aircraft
         design.com or you can quickly write your own.
             The second design example uses hand calculations only for the pre-layout
        activities including initial sizing and selection of T/ W and W/ S. For the rest
        of the example, the author's RDS-Student program was used. RDS-Student
        was written to permit students to analyze and, most important, to optimize
        their aircraft design in a one-semester class. A user-friendly implementation
        of the methods of this book, it is available from AIAA either separately or
        bundled with the book. Further information about RDS-Student and the
        enhanced RDS-Professional can be found at www.aircraftdesign.com or
        www.aiaa.org.
             The author recommends that students do their initial sizing and other
        pre-layout activities by hand as shown here, before being permitted to use
        RDS-Student or any other "canned" design program. Then, use the computer
        for the laborious "number-crunching" of sizing, performance, and trade studies.

� 24.2       Single-Sear Aerobatic Homeb u i lt
          This design represents an aircraft that the author hopes to build and fly
      some day. It would provide fun weekend aerobatic flying for the occasional
      pilot and would offer better performance than the Great Lakes Biplane, but
      without the touchy handling qualities of the Pitts Special.
          The design is fairly classical in layout but is based around quick fabrica­
      tion techniques using moldless foam-fiberglass sandwich construction. This
     permits rapid "garage" fabrication of a one-of-a-kind aircraft. Also, the
     selected engine is already set up for aerobatic flight, which should minimize
     the installation effort.
          One interesting result of the sizing and optimization presented next is
     that the wing loading required for the desired no-flaps stall speed has strongly
     biased the aspect-ratio optimization, leading to a lower-than-expected
    optimal aspect ratio. This looks odd until one notes that the total wing
    span is quite normal after optimization-it is the chord length that is
    excessive, to provide enough wing area.
         (Special note to homebuilders concerning the first example-DON'T
    BUILD IT! This is a first-pass conceptual design only. It would take signifi­
    cant design and analysis effort by an experienced designer before this
    concept could be built and safely flown.)

     Lig htweight Su percru ise Fighter
    This second design example is a lightweight fighter, similar to the original
concept for the F- 16 but with newer technologies and additional capabilities.
It would operate as a cheap, "low-end" complement to the F-22, much as the
F- 16 did for the F-15. Design requirements reflect assumed improvements to
the F- 16's capabilities, with the addition of sustained supersonic cruise on dry
power ("supercruise") . Also, relatively short takeoff and landing requirements
are imposed. To avoid unpleasant conversations with government personnel,
no attempt was made to apply stealth shaping or treatments but they would
undoubtedly be present in an actual aircraft designed for this mission.
    The selected design incorporates one unproven technology, the variable
dihedral vertical tail. This author-patented concept [l ?O] purports to control
the rearward shift in aerodynamic center as the aircraft accelerates to super­
sonic flight by converting from a V tail subsonically to upright vertical tails
supersonically. This reduces trim drag and enhances maneuverability, as
was found during studies at Rockw�ll. However, the obvious weight
penalty makes it of marginal utility. It is shown here to illustrate how
designers handle a new technology for which no prior experience can be
applied. And, it's a fun design example!
    Such a technology study is very common in early conceptual design. The
impact of such a new technology on aerodynamics, weights, propulsion, etc.,
is estimated as best as possible, and the aircraft is sized and optimized. The
resulting aircraft is then compared to a baseline design that does not incor­
porate the new technology to determine if the new idea should be pursued.
   (Homebuilders: don't build this one either!)

                           AIRCRAFT DESIGN

           Design Analysis


              From the dimensions and areas measured from the design layout, this
           initial design layout of the DR-3 aircraft was analyzed using the methods
           presented in thi s book. Analysis as described below included aerodynamics,
           weights, propulsion, sizing, performance, and cost. Also, a TIW- WIS carpet
           plot   was   prepared to optimi ze the design.         The   author's   RDS -Student
           computer program was used for the "number-crunching . " This analysis
           could have been done by hand l ike the first design example. Students should
           be capable of analysis using only a pocket calculator before they are
           permitted to use RDS or any other "canned" computer program.
              RDS - S tudent is available from AIAA along with thi s textbook, and
          includes the complete DR-3 sample design files as described below. RDS­
          S tudent and the more-powerful RDS -Professional are described at the
          author' s website, www. aircraftdesign. com, where additional RDS data files
          are available for download.


          Aerodynamic Lift and Drag


            Aerodynamic      analysis   inputs   to   RDS ,   including    surface   areas   and
          geometry for wings, tails, fuselage, canopy, and boundary-layer diverter, are
          shown on the next two pages. Fuselage and canopy equivalent diameters
          were determined from maximum cross- section areas . Skin friction drag
          analysis assumed fully turbulent flow over camouflage paint. Dlq for the
          missile was i nput based upon the AIM-9 data in Fig. 1 2 . 2 5 , and a cannon
          port Dlq of 0.2 was input as a constant value from zero to Mach 2. Leakage
          and protuberance drag of six percent was assumed.
             For wave drag analysis, the maximum total cross section area was
         estimated at 20.9 square feet { 1 . 94 sq.m. ) , Jess 3 . 8 3 for capture area { 0 . 3 6
         sq.m. ) , or a n e t of 1 7 .07 { 1 . 5 8 sq.m. ) square feet. A supersonic wave drag
         empirical factor (Ew ct) of 2 . 0 was assumed, typical of an aircraft designed
         with some attention to area ruling.
             Maximum lift was estimated by adj usting the airfoil maximum lift for the
         effects of the assumed automatic leading- and trailing-edge maneuver flap s .
         F o r a 64-series airfoil, Ci-max is about 0 . 82, and from Table 1 2 . 1 , delta-Y i s
         about 1 . 2 8 . Using Table 1 2 . 2 the lift adjustment for trailing-edge plain flaps
         is about 0 . 9 , and for leading-edge flaps, about 0 . 3 . With hinge line angles of
         1 0 and 39 deg, Eq. ( 1 2. 2 1 ) gives a delta Ci-max of about 0.82, giving an
         adj usted airfoil Ci-max of 1 . 64. For landing, a CL-max value of 1 . 8 was assumed
         based on data for modern fighters with leading edge flap s .
            T h e following pages include a sample of the parasite drag calculation fo r
         o n e altitude a n d velocity, t h e total parasite drag as a function of speed and
         altitude, the parameters determined for calculation of drag-due-to-lift factor
         CK'), a plot of the resulting K versus speed and lift coefficient, and drag
        polars and LID ratios for the DR- 3 .

Weights


    Weights analysis for the DR-3 was done using the fighter equations in
Chapter 1 5 , with adj ustments for composite material usage as in Table 1 5 .4.
The as-drawn takeoff weight of 1 6 ,480 lb { 7475 kg ) was used as the
structural design weight, with ultimate load factor of Nz=7 . 3 3 x 1 . 5 , or 1 1 .
Required dimensions and areas, such as the control surface area for the wing,
were measured from the drawing.
    The V-tail was analyzed with the horizontal tail statistical equation,
because a V-tail i s loaded for trim and maneuvers much like a horizontal tai l .
T h e analysis w a s based o n t h e true area and aspect ratio of the surface, i . e . ,
       2
9 0 ft { 8.4 sq.m } , and A = 6 . 5 (equivalent). T o account for the variable
dihedral mechanism and structural requirements, a 200 lb { 90.7-kg } weight
penalty was added as a part of the miscellaneous empty weight.
    For the landing gear, it was assumed that landing weight equals design
takeoff weight, and gear load factor was_ assumed to be 4.
    For engine cooling it was assumed that a shroud covers the entire engine,
so the shroud length is 14 ft { 4.3 m } . Engine control length was estimated
from the drawing as 1 8 . 3 ft { 5 .6 m } . To allow for the extra weight of the
2- D vectoring nozzle, an additional 400 lb { 1 8 1 .4 kg } was added to the
miscellaneous empty weight.
    In the absence of better data, installed avionics weight of 990 lb { 449 kg }
was guessed      using Table      1 1 .6 .   However,   the RDS program        requires
uninstalled avionics weight, which it uses to estimate installed avionics
weight, so Eq. ( 1 5 . 2 1 ) was used to back out an uninstalled weight of 727 lb
{ 3 30 kg ) .
   The gun was assumed to always stay with the aircraft and so was treated
as an addition to the miscellaneous empty weight of 400 lb { 1 8 1 .4 kg } .
   The following pages provide the complete weights assumptions and
inputs, followed by the resulting summary weights statement.                The empty
weight for the as-drawn takeoff weight of 1 6,480 lb                 { 7475 kg }    was
determined to be 1 0947 .2 lb { 4965 . 6 kg } , somewhat above the prelimi nary
prediction of 1 07 8 8 lb { 4893 kg } used for initial sizing.
   Weights estimation inputs and results are tabulated below .

Propulsion


   The DR-3 uses the afterbuming turbofan engine in Appendix E . 1 , with an
assumed reduction in specific fuel consumption ( S FC or C) of 20 percent to
adjust for " advanced technology . " The uninstalled engine, which already
includes reasonable allowances for the installation effects of bleed and
power extraction, was loaded into RDS data arrays of maximum afterbuming
thrust and SFC, and maximum dry power thrust and SFC . Then installation
values for inlet recovery, inlet drag, and nozzle drag w ere input and used to
calculate installed thrust and SFC throughout the flight envelope.
 The engine was assumed to be "rubber," i . e . , it could be scaled to virtually
any size and thrust to meet the thrust needs of the sized aircraft. This is
common in early design studies when we c an assume that a new engine will
be designed and built for our aircraft design. Note that one should normally
scale a "rubber" engine by no more than about 20-30 % , and this example
required far greater scaling (downward in size). In a real design study,
learning that the proposed engine was far too large would lead to selection of
a different engine, not to a scaling of that engine by a factor of 50% or more !
   Following are the input assumptions, analysis c alculations, and graphs of
the installed thrust and SFC for the unscaled engine. Note that scaling of the
engine i s done during mission sizing for this design example.

Stability and Control


    An advanced fighter concept such as this would use relaxed static
stability with an active, fully computerized flight control system as described
in Chapters 1 1 and 1 6 . For such a concept, early first-order stability and
control calculations are not so critical                       because the aircraft's handling
qualities will be determined largely by the computer programming, provided
that basic requirements including tail sizes and e.g. location are met and the
aircraft has adequately sized control surfaces.
    Tails were sized using hi storical volume coefficients (Chapter 6) and
should prove sufficient, pending detailed calculations and/or wind tunnel
testing. The wing location was set to give approximately the desired stability
level, in this case slightly negative at subsonic speeds and not too positive
(i.e. , relaxed stability)             at supersonic speeds .       From the    e.g.   estimated
previously, we can use the first-order methods of Chapter 16 to estimate
neutral point and hence, static margin. This was done using RDS-Student,
with results at M0. 6 as detailed below and as graphed below as a function of
Mach number. As can be seen, this design is just slightly unstable at
subsonic speeds-good for minimizing trim drag. Supersonically, the design
is too stable but this analysis does not take into account the variable dihedral
tails. When brought to an upright position they will destabilize the aircraft
preventing a trim drag penalty-exactly as intended.
    Following the static margin i s a subsonic trim plot showing a slight
instability . Note that it takes only a small elevator deflection to trim.

Refined Sizing and Performance


   Next the DR-3          was   sized to the   design mission and the required
performance values were calculated, using the methods of this book as
implemented in the RDS -Student computer program. A detailed mi ssion
model was developed in RDS matching the exact mis sion profile given with
the design requirements. Several assumptions and estimations were used.
Takeoff was as sumed to consist of five minutes at military (dry) power.
Cruise was performed at M0. 8 5 at 45 ,000 ft { 1 3 7 1 6 m } , determined from the
range optimization plot to maximize range per unit fuel weight used. Best
loiter speed at sea level was determined to be M0. 29, found using the loiter
optimization plot, which calculates seconds of loiter per unit fuel weight
used. A 5 0 n-miles ( 92 . 6 km } range credit was assumed for the descent from
high-altitude cruise down to sea level.
   Mission sizing, as detailed below, resulted in a resized takeoff gros s
weight of 1 7062 l b { 7 7 3 9 kg } , vs our original as-drawn weight of 1 6 ,480 lb
( 7475 kg } . Thi s i s closer than one would usually hope for, and probably
reflects luck more than skill !
   After the mission sizing results are two trade studies, one of the sizing
effect of a change in range requirement and one of the effect of an increase
or decrease in engine fuel consumption. These were automatically done with
the RDS -Professional program. However, these could h ave been done w ith
RDS-Stu dent by parametrically changing range or SFC and rerunning the
sizing calculation, recording the resulting sized takeoff gros s weights, and
plotting the answers in a format similar to these.
   Performance calculations were done at a combat weight of 0.89 times
takeoff weight, which is the weight at the end of cruise (beginning of
combat) . The RDS program was again used to perform the calculations and
make the graphs, but the s ame results would be obtained using a pocket
calculator and the methods of this book (and a lot of time ! ) .
   Performance calculations follow the sizing results , including takeoff,
landing, Ps, turn rate, and acceleration. Also included are plots of flight
envelope, specific range, rate of climb, Ps, and turn rate .
   Note    that   while    most    performance     requirements    were   met,   the
requirement for acceleration from M . 9 to M l .4 in 30 s was not met by the
baseline DR-3 design ! Either the thrust will have to be increased, or the
requirement will have to be relaxed. This is further discussed in the carpet
plot optimization at the end of this design example.

             AIRCRAFT DESIGN

T/W- W/S Optimization

   Optimization of thrust-to-weight ratio and wing loading was done using
the carpet plot methods of Chapter 1 9 . Parametric variations of plus-and­
minus 1 0 and 20% were made about the as-drawn baseline of TIW=0.98 and
            2
W/S =56 lb/f { 27 3 . l kg/sq . m } . RDS was again used.
   For variations in TIW, it was assumed that engine thrust varies directly
with TIW. Uninstalled engine weight was assumed to v ary by the 1 . 1 power
of the relative change in thrust [see Eq. ( 1 0 . 3 ) ] . The aerodynamic effect of a
change in TIW, largely the increase in nacelle wetted area, was assumed to be
proportional to engine flow path area and therefore proportional to TIW.
  The aerodynamic and weight impacts of variations in WIS were determined
assuming that wing area varies inversely with wing loading. Tail area was
varied by the 3/2 power of the relative change in wing area to keep tail
volume constant [see Eqs. ( 6 . 2 8 and 6.29)] . The change in wave drag due to
the change in wing size was estimated by changing the maximum cross
sectional area (Amax) proportional to the change in wing area, weighted to the
wing ' s baseline percentage of total cross-section area.
 For each combination of parametric variations in TIW and WIS (25 in all),
the RDS input matrices were revised. The aircraft was reanalyzed for
aerodynamics and weights , and the engine thrust was scaled. Then the sizing,
cost, and performance analysis were rerun as tabulated below. A carpet plot
was prepared using the RDS -Professional program to save time, but could
have been done by hand.
  The optimum airplane that meets all requirements is shown on the carpet
plot at the intersection of the lines labeled " 2-Landing " and " 7 -Acceleration"
(30 sec . ) . It weighs 1 9, 3 00 lb { 42 1 8 kg } and has a T/W of I . I and a WIS of
5 9 { 2 8 8 ) . This weight is 1 7 % greater than the as-drawn DR-3 weight, but
remember that the baseline could not meet the acceleration requirement. B y
relaxing the requirement fo r acceleration fr o m Mach 0 . 9 t o 1 .4 from 30 s to
50 s , the weight of an optimal aircraft fully meeting all other requirements
drops to 1 5 ,600 lb ( 7070 kg } . Also, this changes the optimal TIW to 0.9 and
wing loading to 54 { 264 } and is shown at the intersection of the lines " 2 -
Landing " and " 8-Acceleration" (50 s ) . This is a 1 9% reduction in sized
takeoff gross weight from the aircraft that can meet the acceleration
requirement. This will produce a considerable cost savings for the relaxation
of that one requirement.
 Just for fun, the RDS -Professional Multivariable Optimizer was run to
determine what additional weight savings could be obtained by optimizing
for sweep, aspect ratio , taper ratio , and thickness as well as T/W and WIS.
This produced an optimized weight of 1 5 , 242 lb { 69 1 4 kg } , 2% less than the
optimum found with a T/W- WIS c arpet plot. This indicates that the wing
planform chosen for the DR-3 using the methods of this book was fairly
close to optimal already.      However, this further 2 % weight savings i s
obtained for free, resulting just fr o m slight changes t o the wing geometry.

                                            Typical Engine
                                            Performance
                                            Curves



    T
             his appendix contains performance curves for three different types of
             aircraft engines: an afterburning turbofan, a high-bypass-ratio turbo­
             fan, and a turboprop. Although not identical to any currently in pro­
    duction, these engines are representative of advanced technology suitable for
    use in aircraft design studies. The engines may be scaled using the scaling
    laws presented in Chapter 10.
         These curves were generated using Version 2.0 of the engine-cycle analy­
    sis programs ONX and OFFX that are based on the methods contained in the
    AIAA Education Series textbook, Aircraft Engine Design, by Jack
    D. Mattingly, William H. Heiser, and Daniel H. Daley. Both the textbook
    and the programs with their user guide are available from the publisher.
    The author would like to thank Jack Mattingly for preparation of these
    engine performance curves.
        Note: All altitudes are in feet.

QUESTIONS
Following are the author's suggested homework/examination questions for
each chapter. The exact questions should be changed a bit to ensure that
the students don't find the answers online!
    Another option, favored by the author, is to have the students do a com­
plete design project similar to the design examples of Chapter 21 . This would
test the students' understanding of the design and analysis methods pre­
sented throughout the book and give them a better picture of the overall
design process. A sample RFP is included at the end of this section.
    This author recommends that the students work individually for their first
exposure to aircraft design, each doing an entire design project rather than
working as a team. This ensures that they will experience the whole design pro­
cess rather than focus on the part of the process that they already understand.
    The author's RDSwi n _student aircraft design software program was
specifically developed to reduce the amount of time spent doing "number­
crunching" design analysis. This allows the students to do trade studies
and carpet plots in a one-semester class, and to conclude their design
project reports with the improvements they'd make for the "Dash-Two."

Author's Note and Chapter 1
1 . 1 Raymer seems to think that some people make especially good designers,
      whereas a different tyge of person is probably better as a design analyst.
      Others feel that a well-rounded engineer can and should be equally good
      at both. Choose and defend either belief. There is no right answer; your
      grade depends on demonstrating an understanding of design.
1.2 True/false? Why? "The ability to use a top-end CAD system is probably
    the single most important skill required to be successful in conceptual
    design today."

Sample Request for Proposal Supersonic Business Jet RFP
   The customer seeks a conceptual design study of a supersonic business j et
to take to investors, with intention to develop, test, and produce it as a
l 008   Aircraft Des ig n : A Conceptual Approach

        commercial venture. The following requirements are not firm, and sugges ­
        tions are welcome. (In other words, there just might be some "requirements"
        given that the students should determine are excessive or unwise!)
        • Nonstop supersonic cruise from Paris to New York at Mach 1.8 or greater
        • Divert distance of 200 n miles {370 km}
        • Eight passengers and crew of two
                                                                         3
        • 400-lb { 1 8 1 -kg} baggage in cargo hold of 80 cubic ft {2.3 m }

        • 5000-ft {l,524-m} takeoff balanced field length and landing field length

        • 5000-fpm {l,524-mpm} rate of climb at sea level

        • 140-kt {259-km/h} approach speed

        • 1 10-kt {204-km/h} stall speed

        • Descend from cruising altitude to 1 5,000 ft {4572 m} in less than 5 min

        • Meet FAA and ICAO requirements and specifications


            Students shall present the following in report form:
        Assessment of requirements
        Design sketches (at least four)
        Rationale for selection
        Initial sizing, selection of T/ W, W/ S, and wing geometry
        Design layout
        Analysis: Aero, Weights, Propulsion
        Sizing and performance
        Trade studies: range, payload, cruise speed, etc . . . . (at least one!)
        Optional: Carpet plot- T/ W and W/ S
        Optional: Development and production cost
        Summary and next step
